The electronic properties of graphene

A. H. Castro Neto1, F. Guinea2, N. M. R. Peres3, K. S. Novoselov4, and A. K. Geim4 Affiliation: 1Department of Physics, Boston University, 590 Commonwealth Avenue, Boston, MA 02215,USA Affiliation: 2Instituto de Ciencia de Materiales de Madrid. CSIC. Cantoblanco. E-28049 Madrid, Spain Affiliation: 3Center of Physics and Department of Physics, Universidade do Minho, P-4710-057, Braga, Portugal Affiliation: 4Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Manchester, Manchester, M13 9PL, UK
August 24, 2026
Abstract

This article reviews the basic theoretical aspects of graphene, a one atom thick allotrope of carbon, with unusual two-dimensional Dirac-like electronic excitations. The Dirac electrons can be controlled by application of external electric and magnetic fields, or by altering sample geometry and/or topology. We show that the Dirac electrons behave in unusual ways in tunneling, confinement, and integer quantum Hall effect. We discuss the electronic properties of graphene stacks and show that they vary with stacking order and number of layers. Edge (surface) states in graphene are strongly dependent on the edge termination (zigzag or armchair) and affect the physical properties of nanoribbons. We also discuss how different types of disorder modify the Dirac equation leading to unusual spectroscopic and transport properties. The effects of electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions in single layer and multilayer graphene are also presented.

I Introduction

Carbon is the materia prima for life on the planet and the basis of all organic chemistry. Because of the flexibility of its bonding, carbon-based systems show an unlimited number of different structures with an equally large variety of physical properties. These physical properties are, in great part, the result of the dimensionality of these structures. Among systems with only carbon atoms, graphene - a two-dimensional (2D) allotrope of carbon - plays an important role since it is the basis for the understanding of the electronic properties in other allotropes. Graphene is made out of carbon atoms arranged on a honeycomb structure made out of hexagons (see Fig. 1), and can be thought as composed of benzene rings stripped out from their hydrogen atoms [312]. Fullerenes [27] are molecules where carbon atoms are arranged spherically, and hence, from the physical point of view, are zero-dimensional objects with discrete energy states. Fullerenes can be obtained from graphene with the introduction of pentagons (that create positive curvature defects), and hence, fullerenes can be thought as wrapped up graphene. Carbon nanotubes [351, 79] are obtained by rolling graphene along a given direction and reconnecting the carbon bonds. Hence, carbon nanotubes have only hexagons and can be thought as one-dimensional (1D) objects. Graphite, a three dimensional (3D) allotrope of carbon, became widely known to mankind after the invention of the pencil in 1564 [326] and its usefulness as an instrument for writing comes from the fact that graphite is made out of stacks of graphene layers that are weakly coupled by van der Waals forces. Hence, when one presses a pencil against a sheet of paper one is actually producing graphene stacks and, somewhere among them, there could be individual graphene layers. Although graphene is the mother for all these different allotropes and has been presumably produced every time someone writes with a pencil, it was only isolated 440 years after its invention [293]. The reason is that, first, no one actually expected graphene to exist in the free state and, second, even with the benefit of hindsight, no experimental tools existed to search for one-atom-thick-flakes among the pencil debris covering macroscopic areas [133]. Graphene was eventually spotted due to the subtle optical effect it creates on top of a cleverly chosen SiO2 substrate [293] that allows its observation with an ordinary optical microscope [49, 5, 66]. Hence, graphene is relatively straightforward to make, but not so easy to find.

The structural flexibility of graphene is reflected in its electronic properties. The sp2 hybridization between one s-orbital and two p-orbitals leads to a trigonal planar structure with a formation of a σ\sigma-bond between carbon atoms which are separated by 1.421.42 Å. The σ\sigma-band is responsible for the robustness of the lattice structure in all allotropes. Due to the Pauli principle these bands have a filled shell and hence, form a deep valence band. The unaffected p-orbital, which is perpendicular to the planar structure, can bind covalently with neighboring carbon atoms leading to the formation of a π\pi-band. Since each p-orbital has one extra electron, the π\pi-band is half-filled.

Half-filled bands in transition elements have played an important role in the physics of strongly correlated systems since, due to its strong tight binding character, the Coulomb energies are very large, leading to strong collective effects, magnetism, and insulating behavior due to correlation gaps or Mottness [327]. In fact, Linus Pauling proposed in the 1950’s that, on the basis of the electronic properties of benzene, graphene should be a resonant valence bond structure (RVB) [312]. RVB states have become very popular in the literature of transition metal oxides, and particularly in studies of cuprate oxides superconductors [242]. This point of view, should be contrasted with contemporaneous band structure studies of graphene [422] that found it to be a semimetal with unusual linearly dispersing electronic excitations called Dirac electrons. While most of the current experimental data in graphene supports the band structure point of view, the role of the electron-electron interactions in graphene is a subject of intense research.

It was P. R. Wallace who in 1946 wrote the first papers on the band structure of graphene and showed the unusual semimetallic behavior in this material [422]. At that point in time, the thought of a purely 2D structure was a mere fantasy and Wallace’s studies of graphene served him as a starting point to study graphite, a very important material for nuclear reactors in the post-World War II era. During the following years, the study of graphite culminated with the Slonczewski-Weiss-McClure (SWM) band structure of graphite which provided a detailed description of the electronic properties in this material [378, 255] and was very successful in describing the experimental data [256, 385, 428, 55, 387, 258, 101]. Interestingly enough, from 1957 to 1968, the assignment of the electron and hole states within the SWM model were the opposite to what is accepted today. In 1968, Schroeder et al. [360] established the currently accepted location of electron and hole pockets [259]. The SWM model has been revisited in recent years because of its inability to describe the van der Waals-like interactions between graphene planes, a problem that requires the understanding of many-body effects that go beyond the band structure description [344]. These issues, however, do not arise in the context of a single graphene crystal but they show up with great importance when graphene layers are stacked on top of each other, as in the case, for instance, of the bilayer graphene. Stacking can change the electronic properties considerably and the layering structure can be used in order to control the electronic properties.

One of the most interesting aspects of the graphene problem is that its low energy excitations are massless, chiral, Dirac fermions. In neutral graphene the chemical potential crosses exactly the Dirac point. This particular dispersion, that is only valid at low energies, mimics the physics of quantum electrodynamics (QED) for massless fermions except by the fact that in graphene the Dirac fermions move with a speed vFv_{F} which is 300 times smaller than the speed of light, cc. Hence, many of the unusual properties of QED can show up in graphene but at much smaller speeds [74, 200, 199]. Dirac fermions behave in very unusual ways when compared to ordinary electrons if subjected to magnetic fields, leading to new physical phenomena [322, 160] such as the anomalous integer quantum Hall effect (IQHE) measured experimentally [292, 443]. Besides being qualitatively different from the IQHE observed in Si and GaAlAs (heterostructures) devices [392], the IQHE in graphene can be observed at room temperature because of the large cyclotron energies for “relativistic” electrons [295]. In fact, the anomalous IQHE is the trademark of Dirac fermion behavior.

Another particularly interesting feature of Dirac fermions is their insensitivity to external electrostatic potentials due to the so-called Klein paradox, that is, the fact that Dirac fermions can be transmitted with probability one through a classically forbidden region [185, 63]. In fact, Dirac fermions behave in a very unusual way in the presence of confining potentials leading to the phenomenon of zitterbewegung, or jittery motion of the wavefunction [185]. In graphene these electrostatic potentials can be easily generated by disorder. Since disorder is unavoidable in any material, there has been great interest in trying to understand how disorder affects the physics of electrons in graphene and its transport properties. In fact, under certain conditions, Dirac fermions are immune to localization effects observed in ordinary electrons [224] and it has been established experimentally that electrons can propagate without scattering over large distances of the order of micrometers in graphene [293]. The sources of disorder in graphene are many and can vary from ordinary effects commonly found in semiconductors, such as ionized impurities in the Si substrate, to adatoms and various molecules adsorbed in the graphene surface, to more unusual defects such as ripples associated with the soft structure of graphene [261]. In fact, graphene is unique in the sense that it shares properties of soft membranes [276] and at the same time it behaves in a metallic way, so that the Dirac fermions propagate on a locally curved space. Here, analogies with problems of quantum gravity become apparent [118]. The softness of graphene is related with the fact that it has out-of-plane vibrational modes (phonons) that cannot be found in 3D solids. These flexural modes, responsible for the bending properties of graphene, also account for the lack of long range structural order in soft membranes leading the phenomenon of crumpling [276]. Nevertheless, the presence of a substrate or scaffolds that hold graphene in place, can stabilize a certain degree of order in graphene but leaves behind the so-called ripples (which can be viewed as frozen flexural modes).

It was realized very early on that graphene should also present unusual mesoscopic effects [319, 195]. These effects have their origin in the boundary conditions required for the wavefunctions in mesoscopic samples with various types of edges graphene can have [273, 420, 322, 10]. The most studied edges, zigzag and armchair, have drastically different electronic properties. Zigzag edges can sustain edge (surface) states and resonances that are not present in the armchair case. Moreover, when coupled to conducting leads, the boundary conditions for a graphene ribbon strongly affects its conductance and the chiral Dirac nature of the fermions in graphene can be exploited for applications where one can control the valley flavor of the electrons besides its charge, the so-called valleytronics [343]. Furthermore, when superconducting contacts are attached to graphene, they lead to the development of supercurrent flow and Andreev processes characteristic of superconducting proximity effect [169]. The fact that Cooper pairs can propagate so well in graphene attests for the robust electronic coherence in this material. In fact, quantum interference phenomena such as weak localization, universal conductance fluctuations [267], and the Aharonov-Bohm effect in graphene rings have already been observed experimentally [341, 334]. The ballistic electronic propagation in graphene can be used for field effect devices such as p-n [82, 408, 180, 227, 427, 81, 441, 121] and p-n-p [306] junctions, and as “neutrino” billiards [45, 263]. It has also been suggested that Coulomb interactions are considerably enhanced in smaller geometries, such as graphene quantum dots [264], leading to unusual Coulomb blockade effects [134] and perhaps to magnetic phenomena such as the Kondo effect. The amazing transport properties of graphene allow for their use in a plethora of applications ranging from single molecule detection [358, 426] to spin injection [174, 298, 87, 405].

Because of its unusual structural and electronic flexibility, graphene can be tailored chemically and/or structurally in many different ways: deposition of metal atoms [411, 61] or molecules [358, 426, 226] on top; intercalation (as it is done in graphite intercalated compounds [106, 107, 399]); incorporation of nitrogen and/and boron in its structure [324, 248] (in analogy with what has been done in nanotubes [390]); using different substrates that modify the electronic structure [446, 414, 138, 117, 62, 96]. The control of graphene properties can be extended in new directions allowing for creation of graphene-based systems with magnetic and superconducting properties [410] that are unique in their 2D properties. Although the graphene field is still in its infancy, the scientific and technological possibilities of this new material seem to be unlimited. The understanding and control of the properties of this material can open doors for a new frontier in electronics. As the current status of the experiment and potential applications have recently been reviewed [134], in this article we mostly concentrate on the theory and more technical aspects of electronic properties of this exciting new material.

II Elementary electronic properties of graphene

II.1 Single layer: tight-binding approach

Graphene is made out of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal structure as shown in Fig. 2. The structure is not a Bravais lattice but can be seen as a triangular lattice with a basis of two atoms per unit cell. The lattice vectors can be written as:

II.1.1 Cyclotron mass

The energy dispersion (7) resembles the energy of ultra-relativistic particles; these particles are quantum mechanically described by the massless Dirac equation (see section II.2 for more on this analogy). An immediate consequence of this massless Dirac-like dispersion is a cyclotron mass that depends on the electronic density as its square root [292, 443]. The cyclotron mass is defined, within the semiclassical approximation [29], as

m∗=12​π​[∂A⁡(E)∂E]E=EF,m^{\ast}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\frac{\partial A(E)}{\partial E}\right]_{E=E_{F}}\,, (10)

with A⁡(E)A(E) the area in k−k-space enclosed by the orbit and given by:

A⁡(E)=π​q​(E)2=π​E2vF2.A(E)=\pi q(E)^{2}=\pi\frac{E^{2}}{v_{F}^{2}}\,. (11)

Using (11) in (10) one obtains:

m∗=EFvF2=kFvF.m^{\ast}=\frac{E_{F}}{v^{2}_{F}}=\frac{k_{F}}{v_{F}}\,. (12)

The electronic density, nn, is related to the Fermi momentum, kFk_{F}, as kF2/π=nk^{2}_{F}/\pi=n (with contributions from the two Dirac points 𝑲{\bm{K}} and 𝑲′{\bm{K}^{\prime}} and spin included) which leads to:

m∗=πvF​n.m^{\ast}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{v_{F}}\sqrt{n}\,. (13)

Fitting (13) to the experimental data (see Fig.4) provides an estimation for the Fermi velocity and the hopping parameter as vF≈106​ms-1v_{F}\approx 10^{6}\,\textrm{ms${}^{-1}$} and t≈3​eVt\approx 3\,\textrm{eV}, respectively. The experimental observation of the n\sqrt{n} dependence of the cyclotron mass provides evidence for the existence of massless Dirac quasiparticles in graphene [187, 292, 443, 97] - the usual parabolic (Schrödinger) dispersion implies a constant cyclotron mass.

II.1.2 Density of states

The density of states per unit cell, derived from (6), is given in Fig. 5 for both t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and t′≠0t^{\prime}\neq 0, showing in both cases a semimetallic behavior [422, 40]. For t′=0t^{\prime}=0 it is possible to derive an analytical expression for the density of states per unit cell, which has the form [176]:

where 𝐅⁡(π/2,x)\mathbf{F}(\pi/2,x) is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Close to the Dirac point the dispersion is approximated by (7) and the expression for the density of states per unit cell is given by (with a degeneracy of four included):

ρ⁡(E)=2​Acπ​|E|vF2\rho(E)=\frac{2A_{c}}{\pi}\frac{|E|}{v^{2}_{F}}\, (15)

where AcA_{c} is the unit cell area given by Ac=3​3​a2/2A_{c}=3\sqrt{3}a^{2}/2. It is worth noting that the density of states for graphene is very different from the density of states of carbon nanotubes [353, 352]. The latter show 1/E1/\sqrt{E} singularities due to the 1D nature of their electronic spectrum, which comes about due to the quantization of the momentum in the direction perpendicular to the tube axis. From this perspective, graphene nanoribbons, which also have momentum quantization perpendicular to the ribbon length, have properties very similar to carbon nanotubes.

II.2 Dirac fermions

Let us consider Hamiltonian (5) with t′=0t^{\prime}=0 and consider the Fourier transform of the electron operators:

an=1Nc∑𝒌e−i𝒌⋅𝑹na(𝒌),,a_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{c}}}\sum_{\bm{k}}e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}}a(\bm{k}),, (16)

where NcN_{c} is the number of unit cells. Using this transformation, let us write the field ana_{n} as a sum of two terms, coming from expanding the Fourier sum around 𝑲′{\bm{K}^{\prime}} and 𝑲{\bm{K}}. This produces an approximation for the representation of the field ana_{n} as a sum of two new fields, written as

an\displaystyle a_{n} ≃\displaystyle\simeq e−i𝑲⋅𝑹na1,n+e−i𝑲′⋅𝑹na2,n,\displaystyle e^{-i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}}a_{1,n}+e^{-i\bm{K}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}}a_{2,n}\,,
bn\displaystyle b_{n} ≃\displaystyle\simeq e−i𝑲⋅𝑹nb1,n+e−i𝑲′⋅𝑹nb2,n,\displaystyle e^{-i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}}b_{1,n}+e^{-i\bm{K}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}}b_{2,n}\,, (17)

where the index i=1i=1 (i=2i=2) refers to the K (K’) point. These new fields, ai,na_{i,n} and bi,nb_{i,n} are assumed to vary slowly over the unit cell. The procedure for deriving a theory that is valid close to the Dirac point consists in using this representation in the tight-binding Hamiltonian and expanding the operators up to a linear order in 𝜹\bm{\delta}. In the derivation one uses the fact that ∑𝜹e±i𝑲⋅𝜹=∑𝜹e±i𝑲′⋅𝜹=0.\sum_{\bm{\delta}}e^{\pm i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{\delta}}=\sum_{\bm{\delta}}e^{\pm i\bm{K}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{\delta}}=0. After some straightforward algebra we arrive at [361]:

H\displaystyle H ≃\displaystyle\simeq −t∫dxdyΨ^1†(𝒓)[(03​a​(1−i​3)/4−3a(1+i3)/40)∂x+(03​a​(−i−3)/4−3a(i−3)/40)∂y]Ψ^1(𝒓)\displaystyle-t\int dxdy\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}_{1}(\bm{r})\left[\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&3a(1-i\sqrt{3})/4\\ -3a(1+i\sqrt{3})/4&0\end{array}\right)\partial_{x}\right.+\left.\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&3a(-i-\sqrt{3})/4\\ -3a(i-\sqrt{3})/4&0\end{array}\right)\partial_{y}\right]\hat{\Psi}_{1}(\bm{r}) (28)
+\displaystyle+ Ψ^2†(𝒓)[(03​a​(1+i​3)/4−3a(1−i3)/40)∂x+(03​a​(i−3)/4−3a(−i−3)/40)∂y]Ψ^2(𝒓)\displaystyle\hskip 48.36958pt\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}_{2}(\bm{r})\left[\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&3a(1+i\sqrt{3})/4\\ -3a(1-i\sqrt{3})/4&0\end{array}\right)\partial_{x}+\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&3a(i-\sqrt{3})/4\\ -3a(-i-\sqrt{3})/4&0\end{array}\right)\partial_{y}\right]\hat{\Psi}_{2}(\bm{r})
=\displaystyle= −ivF∫dxdy(Ψ^1†(𝒓)𝝈⋅∇Ψ^1(𝒓)+Ψ^2†(𝒓)𝝈∗⋅∇Ψ^2(𝒓)),\displaystyle-iv_{F}\int dxdy\left(\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}_{1}(\bm{r})\bm{\sigma}\cdot\nabla\hat{\Psi}_{1}(\bm{r})+\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}_{2}(\bm{r})\bm{\sigma}^{*}\cdot\nabla\hat{\Psi}_{2}(\bm{r})\right)\,,

with Pauli matrices 𝝈=(σx,σy)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}), 𝝈∗=(σx,−σy)\bm{\sigma}^{*}=(\sigma_{x},-\sigma_{y}), and Ψ^i†=(ai†,bi†)\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}_{i}=(a^{\dagger}_{i},b^{\dagger}_{i}) (i=1,2i=1,2). It is clear that the effective Hamiltonian (28) is made of two copies of the massless Dirac-like Hamiltonian, one holding for 𝒑\bm{p} around 𝑲\bm{K} and other for 𝒑\bm{p} around 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime}. Notice that, in first quantized language, the two-component electron wavefunction, ψ⁡(𝐫)\psi({\bf r}), close to the K point, obeys the 2D Dirac equation:

−ivF𝝈⋅∇ψ(𝐫)=Eψ(𝐫).\displaystyle-iv_{F}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\nabla\psi({\bf r})=E\psi({\bf r})\,. (29)

The wavefunction, in momentum space, for the momentum around 𝑲\bm{K} has the form:

ψ±,𝐊​(𝐤)=12​(e−iθ𝐤/2±ei​θ𝐤/2),\psi_{\pm,{\bf K}}({\bf k})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{-i\theta_{{\bf k}}/2}\\ \pm e^{i\theta_{{\bf k}}/2}\end{array}\right)\,, (30)

for HK=vF​𝝈⋅𝐤H_{K}=v_{F}\bm{\sigma}\cdot{\bf k}, where the ±\pm signs correspond to the eigenenergies E=±vF​kE=\pm v_{F}k, that is, for the π\pi and π∗\pi^{*} band, respectively, and θ𝐤\theta_{{\bf k}} is given by (9). The wavefunction for the momentum around 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} has the form:

ψ±,𝐊′​(𝐤)=12​(ei​θ𝐤/2±e−iθ𝐤/2),\psi_{\pm,{\bf K^{\prime}}}({\bf k})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}e^{i\theta_{{\bf k}}/2}\\ \pm e^{-i\theta_{{\bf k}}/2}\end{array}\right)\,, (31)

for HK′=vF​𝝈∗⋅𝐤H_{K^{\prime}}=v_{F}\bm{\sigma}^{*}\cdot{\bf k}. Notice that the wavefunctions at 𝐊{\bf K} and 𝐊′{\bf K^{\prime}} are related by time reversal symmetry: if we set the origin of coordinates in momentum space in the M-point of the BZ (see Fig.2), time reversal becomes equivalent to a reflection along the kxk_{x} axis, that is, (kx,ky)→(kx,−ky)(k_{x},k_{y})\to(k_{x},-k_{y}). Also note that if the phase θ\theta is rotated by 2​π2\pi the wavefunction changes sign indicating a phase of π\pi (in the literature this is commonly called a Berry’s phase). This change of phase by π\pi under rotation is characteristic of spinors. In fact, the wavefunction is a two component spinor.

A relevant quantity used to characterize the eigenfunctions is their helicity defined as the projection of the momentum operator along the (pseudo)spin direction. The quantum mechanical operator for the helicity has the form:

h^=12​𝝈⋅𝒑|𝒑|.\hat{h}=\frac{1}{2}{\bm{\sigma}}\cdot\frac{\bm{p}}{|\bm{p}|}\,. (32)

It is clear from the definition of h^\hat{h} that the states ψ𝑲​(𝒓)\psi_{\bm{K}}(\bm{r}) and ψ𝑲′​(𝒓)\psi_{\bm{K}^{\prime}}(\bm{r}) are also eigenstates of h^\hat{h}:

h^​ψ𝑲​(𝒓)=±12​ψ𝑲​(𝒓),\hat{h}\psi_{\bm{K}}(\bm{r})=\pm\frac{1}{2}\psi_{\bm{K}}(\bm{r}), (33)

and an equivalent equation for ψ𝑲′​(𝒓)\psi_{\bm{K}^{\prime}}(\bm{r}) with inverted sign. Therefore electrons (holes) have a positive (negative) helicity. Equation (33) implies that 𝝈\bm{\sigma} has its two eigenvalues either in the direction of (⇑\Uparrow) or against (⇓\Downarrow) the momentum 𝒑{\bm{p}}. This property says that the states of the system close to the Dirac point have well defined chirality or helicity. Notice that chirality is not defined in regards to the real spin of the electron (that has not yet appeared in the problem) but to a pseudo-spin variable associated with the two components of the wavefunction. The helicity values are good quantum numbers as long as the Hamiltonian (28) is valid. Therefore the existence of helicity quantum numbers holds only as an asymptotic property, which is well defined close to the Dirac points 𝑲\bm{K} and 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime}. Either at larger energies or due to the presence of a finite t′t^{\prime} the helicity stops being a good quantum number.

II.2.1 Chiral Tunneling and Klein paradox

In this section we want to address the scattering of chiral electrons in two dimensions by a square barrier [200, 196]. The one dimensional scattering of chiral electrons was discussed earlier in the context of carbon nanotubes [24, 260]

We start by noticing that by a gauge transformation the wavefunction (30) can be written as:

ψ𝑲​(𝒌)=12​(1±ei​θk).\psi_{\bm{K}}(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ \pm e^{i\theta_{k}}\end{array}\right)\,. (34)

We further assume that the scattering does not mix the momenta around 𝑲\bm{K} and 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} points. In Fig. 6 we depict the scattering process due to the square barrier of width DD.

The wavefunction in the different regions can be written in terms of incident and reflected waves. In region I we have:

ψI​(𝒓)\displaystyle\psi_{I}(\bm{r}) =\displaystyle= 12​(1s​ei​ϕ)​ei⁡(kx​x+ky​y)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ se^{i\phi}\end{array}\right)e^{i(k_{x}x+k_{y}y)}
+\displaystyle+ r2​(1s​ei⁡(π−ϕ))​ei⁡(−kx​x+ky​y),\displaystyle\frac{r}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ se^{i(\pi-\phi)}\end{array}\right)e^{i(-k_{x}x+k_{y}y)}\,,

with ϕ=arctan⁡(ky/kx)\phi=\arctan(k_{y}/k_{x}), kx=kF​cos⁡ϕk_{x}=k_{F}\cos\phi, ky=kF​sin⁡ϕk_{y}=k_{F}\sin\phi and kFk_{F} the Fermi momentum. In region II we have:

ψI​I​(𝒓)\displaystyle\psi_{II}(\bm{r}) =\displaystyle= a2​(1s′​ei​θ)​ei⁡(qx​x+ky​y)\displaystyle\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ s^{\prime}e^{i\theta}\end{array}\right)e^{i(q_{x}x+k_{y}y)}
+\displaystyle+ b2​(1s′​ei⁡(π−θ))​ei⁡(−qx​x+ky​y),\displaystyle\frac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ s^{\prime}e^{i(\pi-\theta)}\end{array}\right)e^{i(-q_{x}x+k_{y}y)}\,,

with θ=arctan⁡(ky/qx)\theta=\arctan(k_{y}/q_{x}) and

qx=(V0−E)2/(vF2)−ky2,q_{x}=\sqrt{(V_{0}-E)^{2}/(v_{F}^{2})-k_{y}^{2}}, (47)

and finally in region III we have a transmitted wave only:

ψI​I​I​(𝒓)=t2​(1s​ei​ϕ)​ei⁡(kx​x+ky​y),\psi_{III}(\bm{r})=\frac{t}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ se^{i\phi}\end{array}\right)e^{i(k_{x}x+k_{y}y)}\,, (48)

with s=sgn⁡(E)s={\rm sgn}(E) and s′=sgn⁡(E−V0)s^{\prime}={\rm sgn}(E-V_{0}). The coefficients rr, aa, bb and tt are determined from the continuity of the wavefunction, which implies that the wavefunction has to obey the conditions ψI​(x=0,y)=ψI​I​(x=0,y)\psi_{I}(x=0,y)=\psi_{II}(x=0,y) and ψI​I​(x=D,y)=ψI​I​I​(x=D,y)\psi_{II}(x=D,y)=\psi_{III}(x=D,y). Unlike the Schödinger equation we only need to match the wavefunction but not its derivative. The transmission through the barrier is obtained from T⁡(ϕ)=t​t∗T(\phi)=tt^{\ast} and has the form:

T⁡(ϕ)=cos2⁡θ​cos2⁡ϕ[cos⁡(D​qx)​cos⁡ϕ​cos⁡θ]2+sin2⁡(D​qx)​(−s​s′​sin⁡ϕ​sin⁡θ)2.T(\!\phi\!)\!=\!\frac{\cos^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\phi}{[\cos(Dq_{x})\cos\phi\cos\theta]^{2}\!+\!\sin^{2}(\!Dq_{x}\!)(\!1\!\!-\!\!ss^{\prime}\!\sin\phi\sin\theta\!)^{2}}\,. (49)

This expression does not take into account a contribution from evanescent waves in region II, which is usually negligible, unless the chemical potential in region II is at the Dirac energy (see section IV.9).

Notice that T⁡(ϕ)=T⁡(−ϕ)T(\phi)=T(-\phi) and for values of D​qxDq_{x} satisfying the relation D​qx=n​πDq_{x}=n\pi, with nn an integer, the barrier becomes completely transparent since T⁡(ϕ)=1T(\phi)=1, independently of the value of ϕ\phi. Also, for normal incidence (ϕ→0\phi\rightarrow 0 and θ→0\theta\rightarrow 0) and for any value of D​qxDq_{x} one obtains T⁡(0)=1T(0)=1, and the barrier is again totally transparent. This result is a manifestation of the Klein paradox [185, 63] and does not occur for non-relativistic electrons. In this latter case and for normal incidence, the transmission is always smaller than one. In the limit |V0|≫|E||V_{0}|\gg|E|, eq. (49) has the following asymptotic form

T⁡(ϕ)≃cos2⁡ϕ1−cos2⁡(D​qx)​sin2⁡ϕ.T(\phi)\simeq\frac{\cos^{2}\phi}{1-\cos^{2}(Dq_{x})\sin^{2}\phi}\,. (50)

In Fig. 7 we show the angular dependence of T⁡(ϕ)T(\phi) for two different values of the potential V0V_{0}; it is clear that there are several directions for which the transmission is one. Similar calculations were done for a graphene bilayer [200] with its most distinctive behavior being the absence of tunneling in the forward (ky=0k_{y}=0) direction.

The simplest example of a potential barrier is a square potential discussed previously. When intervalley scattering and the lack of symmetry between sublattices are neglected, a potential barrier shows no reflection for electrons incident in the normal direction [200]. Even when the barrier separates regions where the Fermi surface is electron like on one side and hole like on the other, a normally incident electron continues propagating as a hole with 100% efficiency. This phenomenon is another manifestation of the chirality of the Dirac electrons within each valley, which prevents backscattering in general. The transmission and reflection probabilities of electrons at different angles depend on the potential profile along the barrier. A slowly varying barrier is more efficient in reflecting electrons at non-zero incident angles [82].

Electrons moving through a barrier separating p- and n-doped graphene, a p-n junction, are transmitted as holes. The relation between the velocity and the momentum for a hole is the inverse of that for an electron. This implies that, if the momentum parallel to the barrier is conserved, the velocity of the quasiparticle is inverted. When the incident electrons emerge from a source, the transmitting holes are focused into an image of the source. This behavior is the same as that of photons moving in a medium with negative reflection index [81]. Similar effects can occur in graphene quantum dots, where the inner and outer regions contain electrons and holes, respectively [93]. Note that the fact that barriers do not impede the transmission of normally incident electrons does not preclude the existence of sharp resonances, due to the confinement of electrons with a finite parallel momentum. This leads to the possibility of fabricating quantum dots with potential barriers [374]. Finally, at half-filling, due to disorder graphene can be divided in electron and hole charge puddles [200, 247]. Transport is determined by the transmission across the p-n junctions between these puddles [83, 369]. There is a rapid progress in the measurement of transport properties of graphene ribbons with additional top gates that play the role of tunable potential barriers [163, 427, 180, 309, 227].

A magnetic field and potential fluctuations break both inversion symmetry of the lattice and time reversal symmetry. The combination of these effects break also the symmetry between the two valleys. The transmission coefficient becomes valley dependent, and, in general, electrons from different valleys propagate along different paths. This opens the possibility of manipulating the valley index [408] (valleytronics) in a way similar to the control of the spin in mesoscopic devices (spintronics). For large magnetic fields, a p-n junction separates regions with different quantized Hall conductivities. At the junction, chiral currents can flow at both edges [3], inducing backscattering between the Hall currents at the edges of the sample.

The scattering of electrons near the Dirac point by graphene-superconductor junctions differs from Andreev scattering process in normal metals [403]. When the distance between the Fermi energy and the Dirac energy is smaller than the superconducting gap, the superconducting interaction hybridizes quasiparticles from one band with quasiholes in the other. As in the case of scattering at a p-n junction, the trajectories of the incoming electron and reflected hole (note that hole here is meant as in the BCS theory of superconductivity) are different from those in similar processes in metals with only one type of carrier [46, 239].

II.2.2 Confinement and zitterbewegung

Zitterbewegung, or jittery motion of the wavefunction of the Dirac problem, occurs when one tries to confine the Dirac electrons [185]. Localization of a wavepacket leads, due to the Heisenberg principle, to uncertainty in the momentum. For a Dirac particle with zero rest mass, uncertainty in the momentum translates into uncertainty in the energy of the particle as well (this should be contrasted with the non-relativistic case where the position-momentum uncertainty relation is independent of the energy-time uncertainty relation). Thus, for a ultra-relativistic particle, a particle-like state can have hole-like states in its time evolution. Consider, for instance, if one tries to construct a wave packet at some time t=0t=0, and let us assume, for simplicity, that this packet has a Gaussian shape of width ww with momentum close to 𝐊{\bf K}:

ψ0​(𝐫)=e−r2/(2w2)π​w​ei​𝐊⋅𝐫​ϕ,\displaystyle\psi_{0}({\bf r})=\frac{e^{-r^{2}/(2w^{2})}}{\sqrt{\pi}w}\,e^{i{\bf K}\cdot{\bf r}}\phi\,, (51)

where ϕ\phi is spinor composed of positive energy states (associated with ψ+,𝐊\psi_{+,{\bf K}} of (30)). The eigenfunction of the Dirac equation can be written in terms of the solution (30) as:

ψ⁡(𝐫,t)=∫d2​k(2​π)2​∑a=±1αa,𝐤​ψa,𝐊​(𝐤)​e−i​a​(𝐤⋅𝐫+vF​k​t),\displaystyle\psi({\bf r},t)=\int\frac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}\sum_{a=\pm 1}\alpha_{a,{\bf k}}\psi_{a,{\bf K}}({\bf k})e^{-ia({\bf k}\cdot{\bf r}+v_{F}kt)}\,, (52)

where α±,𝐤\alpha_{\pm,{\bf k}} are Fourier coefficients. We can rewrite (51) in terms of (52) by inverse Fourier transform and find that:

α±,𝐤=πwe−k2w2/2ψ±,𝐊†(𝐤)ϕ.\displaystyle\alpha_{\pm,{\bf k}}=\sqrt{\pi}we^{-k^{2}w^{2}/2}\psi^{{\dagger}}_{\pm,{\bf K}}({\bf k})\phi\,. (53)

Notice that the relative weight of positive energy states with respect to negative energy states, |α+/α−||\alpha_{+}/\alpha_{-}|, given by (30) is one, that is, there are as many positive energy states as negative energy states in a wavepacket. Hence, these will cause the wavefunction to be delocalized at any time t≠0t\neq 0. Thus, a wave packet of electron-like states has hole-like components, a result that puzzled many researchers in the early days of QED [185].

Consider the tight-binding description [320, 84] of Sec. II.1 when a potential ViV_{i} on site 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i} is added to the problem:

He=∑iVi​ni,\displaystyle H_{e}=\sum_{i}V_{i}n_{i}\,, (54)

where nin_{i} is the local electronic density. For simplicity, we assume that the confining potential is 1D, that is, that ViV_{i} vanishes in the bulk but becomes large at the edge of the sample. Let us assume a potential that decays exponentially away from the edges into the bulk with a penetration depth, λ\lambda. In Fig. 8 we show the electronic spectrum for a graphene ribbon of width L=600​aL=600a, in the presence of a confining potential,

V(x)=V0[e−(x−L/2)/λ+e−(L/2−x)/λ],\displaystyle V(x)=V_{0}\left[e^{-(x-L/2)/\lambda}+e^{-(L/2-x)/\lambda}\right]\,, (55)

where xx is the direction of confinement and V0V_{0} the strength of the potential. One can clearly see that in the presence of the confining potential the electron-hole symmetry is broken and, for V0>0V_{0}>0, the hole part of the spectrum is strongly distorted. In particular, for kk close to the Dirac point, we see that the hole dispersion is given by: En,σ=−1​(k)≈−γn​k2−ζn​k4E_{n,\sigma=-1}(k)\approx-\gamma_{n}k^{2}-\zeta_{n}k^{4} where nn is a positive integer, and γn<0\gamma_{n}<0 (γn>0\gamma_{n}>0) for n<N∗n<N^{*} (n>N∗n>N^{*}). Hence, at n=N∗n=N^{*} the hole effective mass diverges (γN∗=0\gamma_{N^{*}}=0) and, by tuning the chemical potential, μ\mu, via a back gate, to the hole region of the spectrum (μ<0\mu<0) one should be able to observe an anomaly in the Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) oscillations. This is how zitterbewegung could manifest itself in magnetotransport.

II.3 Bilayer graphene: tight-binding approach

The tight-binding model developed for graphite can be easily extended to stacks with a finite number of graphene layers. The simplest generalization is a bilayer [252]. A bilayer is interesting because the IQHE shows anomalies, although different from those observed in a single layer [296], and also a gap can open between the conduction and valence band [252]. The bilayer structure, with the AB stacking of 3D graphite, is shown in Fig.9.

The tight-binding Hamiltonian for this problem can be written as:

ℋt.b.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{t.b.}} =\displaystyle= −γ0∑<i,j>m,σ(am,i,σ†bm,j,σ+h.c.)\displaystyle-\gamma_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}<i,j>\\ m,\sigma\end{subarray}}(a_{m,i,\sigma}^{{\dagger}}b_{m,j,\sigma}^{\,}+\text{h.c.}) (56)
−\displaystyle- γ1​∑j,σ(a1,j,σ†​a2,j,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle\gamma_{1}\sum_{j,\sigma}(a_{1,j,\sigma}^{{\dagger}}a_{2,j,\sigma}^{\,}+\text{h.c.}),
−\displaystyle- γ3​∑j,σ(a1,j,σ†​b2,j,σ+a2,j,σ†​b1,j,σ+h.c.)\displaystyle\gamma_{3}\sum_{j,\sigma}(a_{1,j,\sigma}^{{\dagger}}b_{2,j,\sigma}^{\,}+a_{2,j,\sigma}^{{\dagger}}b_{1,j,\sigma}^{\,}+\text{h.c.})
−\displaystyle- γ4​∑j,σ(b1,j,σ†​b2,j,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle\gamma_{4}\sum_{j,\sigma}(b^{{\dagger}}_{1,j,\sigma}b_{2,j,\sigma}+\text{h.c.}),

where am,i,σa_{m,i,\sigma} (bm,i​σb_{m,i\sigma}) annihilates an electron with spin σ\sigma, on sublattice A (B), in plane m=1,2m=1,2, at site 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i}. Here we use the graphite nomenclature for the hopping parameters: γ0=t\gamma_{0}=t is the in-plane hopping energy and γ1\gamma_{1} (γ1=t⟂≈0.4\gamma_{1}=t_{\perp}\approx 0.4 eV in graphite [56, 106]) is the hopping energy between atom A1\text{A}_{1} and atom A2\text{A}_{2} (see Fig. 9), and γ3\gamma_{3} (γ3≈0.3\gamma_{3}\approx 0.3 eV in graphite [56, 106]) is the hopping energy between atom A1\text{A}_{1} (A2\text{A}_{2}) and atom B2\text{B}_{2} (B1\text{B}_{1}), and γ4\gamma_{4} (γ4≈−0.04\gamma_{4}\approx-0.04 eV in graphite [56, 106]) that connects B1\text{B}_{1} and B2\text{B}_{2}.

In the continuum limit, by expanding the momentum close to the K point in the BZ, the Hamiltonian reads,

ℋ=∑𝐤Ψ𝐤†⋅ℋK⋅Ψ𝐤\displaystyle{\cal H}=\sum_{{\bf k}}\Psi_{{\bf k}}^{{\dagger}}\cdot{\cal H}_{K}\cdot\Psi_{{\bf k}} (57)

where (ignoring γ4\gamma_{4} for the time being):

ℋK≡(−VvF​k03​γ3​a​k∗vF​k∗−Vγ100γ1VvF​k3​γ3​a​k0vF​k∗V),{\cal H}_{K}\!\!\equiv\!\!\left(\!\begin{array}[]{cccc}-V&v_{F}k&0&3\gamma_{3}ak^{*}\\ v_{F}k^{*}&-V&\gamma_{1}&0\\ 0&\gamma_{1}&V&v_{F}k\\ 3\gamma_{3}ak&0&v_{F}k^{*}&V\end{array}\!\right)\,, (58)

where k=kx+i​kyk=k_{x}+ik_{y} is a complex number, and we have added VV which is here half the shift in electro-chemical potential between the two layers (this term will appear if a potential bias is applied between the layers), and

Ψ𝐤†=(a1†​(𝐤),a2†​(𝐤),b1†​(𝐤),b2†​(𝐤))\displaystyle\Psi_{{\bf k}}^{{\dagger}}=\left(a^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf k}),a^{{\dagger}}_{2}({\bf k}),b^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf k}),b^{{\dagger}}_{2}({\bf k})\right) (59)

is a four component spinor.

If V=0V=0 and γ3,vF​k≪γ1\gamma_{3},v_{F}k\ll\gamma_{1}, one can eliminate the high energy states perturbatively and write an effective Hamiltonian:

ℋK≡(0vF2​k2γ1+3​γ3​a​k∗vF2​(k∗)2γ1+3​γ3​a​k0).{\cal H}_{K}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\frac{v_{F}^{2}k^{2}}{\gamma_{1}}+3\gamma_{3}ak^{*}\\ \frac{v_{F}^{2}(k^{*})^{2}}{\gamma_{1}}+3\gamma_{3}ak&0\end{array}\right)\,. (60)

The hopping γ4\gamma_{4} leads to a kk dependent coupling between the sublattices or a small renormalization of γ1\gamma_{1}. The same role is played by the inequivalence between sublattices within a layer.

For γ3=0\gamma_{3}=0, (60) gives two parabolic bands, ϵk,±≈±vF2k2/t⟂\epsilon_{k,\pm}\approx\pm v_{F}^{2}k^{2}/t_{\perp} which touch at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 (as shown in Fig.10). The spectrum is electron-hole symmetric. There are two additional bands which start at ±t⟂\pm t_{\perp}. Within this approximation, the bilayer is metallic, with a constant density of states. The term γ3\gamma_{3} changes qualitatively the spectrum at low energies since it introduces a trigonal distortion, or warping, of the bands (notice that this trigonal distortion, unlike the one introduced by large momentum in (8), occurs at low energies). The electron-hole symmetry is preserved but, instead of two bands touching at k=0k=0, we obtain three sets of Dirac-like linear bands. One Dirac point is at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and k=0k=0, while the three other Dirac points, also at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, lie at three equivalent points with a finite momentum. The stability of points where bands touch can be understood using topological arguments [238]. The winding number of a closed curve in the plane around a given point is an integer representing the total number of times that the curve travels counterclockwise around the point so that the wavefunction remains unaltered. The winding number of the point where the two parabolic bands come together for γ3=0\gamma_{3}=0 has winding number +2+2. The trigonal warping term, γ3\gamma_{3}, splits it into a Dirac point at k=0k=0 and winding number −1-1, and three Dirac points at k≠0k\neq 0 and winding numbers +1+1. An in-plane magnetic field, or a small rotation of one layer with respect to the other splits the γ3=0\gamma_{3}=0 degeneracy into two Dirac points with winding number +1+1.

The term VV in (58) breaks the equivalence of the two layers, or, alternatively, inversion symmetry. In this case, the dispersion relation becomes:

ϵ±,𝐤2\displaystyle\epsilon^{2}_{\pm,{\bf k}} =\displaystyle= V2+vF2​k2+t⟂2/2\displaystyle V^{2}+v_{F}^{2}k^{2}+t_{\perp}^{2}/2 (61)
±\displaystyle\pm 4​V2​vF2​k2+t2​vF2​k2+t⟂4/4,\displaystyle\sqrt{4V^{2}v_{F}^{2}k^{2}+t^{2}v_{F}^{2}k^{2}+t_{\perp}^{4}/4}\,,

given rise to the dispersion shown in Fig. 11, and to the opening of a gap close, but not directly at, the K point. For small momenta, and V≪tV\ll t, the energy of the conduction band can be expanded:

ϵk≈V−(2​V​vF2​k2)/t⟂+(vF4​k4)/(2​t⟂2​V).\displaystyle\epsilon_{k}\approx V-(2Vv_{F}^{2}k^{2})/t_{\perp}+(v_{F}^{4}k^{4})/(2t_{\perp}^{2}V)\,. (62)

The dispersion for the valence band can be obtained by replacing ϵk\epsilon_{k} by −ϵk-\epsilon_{k}. The bilayer has a gap at k2≈(2​V2)/vF2k^{2}\approx(2V^{2})/v_{F}^{2}. Notice, therefore, that the gap in the biased bilayer system depends on the applied bias and hence can be measured experimentally [252, 251, 70]. The ability to open a gap makes bilayer graphene most interesting for technological applications.

II.4 Epitaxial graphene

It has been known for a long time that monolayers of graphene could be grown epitaxially on metal surfaces by using catalytic decomposition of hydrocarbons or carbon oxide [366, 112, 64, 304, 375]. When such surfaces are heated, oxygen or hydrogen desorbs, and the carbon atoms form a graphene monolayer. The resulting graphene structures could reach sizes up to a micrometer, with few defects and were characterized by different surface-science techniques and local scanning probes [175]. For example, graphene grown on ruthenium has zigzag edges and also ripples associated with a (10×10)(10\times 10) reconstruction [415].

Graphene can also be formed on the surface of SiC. Upon heating, the silicon from the top layers desorbs, and a few layers of graphene are left on the surface [51, 123, 88, 42, 337, 166, 168]. The number of layers can be controlled by limiting time or temperature of the heating treatment. The quality and the number of layers in the samples depends on the SiC face used for their growth [168] (the carbon terminated surface produces few layers but with a low mobility, whereas the silicon terminated surface produces several layers but with higher mobility). Epitaxially grown multilayers exhibit SdH oscillations with a Berry phase shift of π\pi [41], which is the same as the phase shift for Dirac fermions observed in a single layer as well as for some subbands present in multilayer graphene (see further) and graphite [236]. The carbon layer directly on top of the substrate is expected to be strongly bonded to it, and it shows no π\pi bands [414]. The next layer shows a (6​3×6​3)(6\sqrt{3}\times 6\sqrt{3}) reconstruction due to the substrate, and has graphene properties. An alternate route to produce few layers graphene is based on synthesis from nanodiamonds [9].

Angle resolved photo-emission experiments (ARPES) show that epitaxial graphene grown on SiC has linearly dispersing quasiparticles (Dirac fermions) [447, 301, 54], in agreement with the theoretical expectation. Nevertheless, these experiments show that the electronic properties can change locally in space indicating a certain degree of inhomogeneity due to the growth method [446]. Similar inhomogeneities due to disorder in the c-axis orientation of graphene planes is observed in graphite [445]. Moreover, graphene grown this way is heavily doped due to the charge transfer from the substrate to the graphene layer (with the chemical potential well above the Dirac point) and therefore all samples have strong metallic character with large electronic mobilities [41, 168]. There is also evidence for strong interaction between a substrate and the graphene layer leading to the appearance of gaps at the Dirac point [446]. Indeed, gaps can be generated by the breaking of the sublattice symmetry and, as in the case of other carbon based systems such as polyacethylene [393, 394], it can lead to soliton-like excitations [186, 179]. Multilayer graphene grown on SiC have also been studied with ARPES [302, 301, 53] and the results seem to agree quite well with band structure calculations [250]. Spectroscopy measurements also show the transitions associated with Landau levels [347], and weak localization effects at low magnetic fields, also expected for Dirac fermions [430]. Local probes reveal a rich structure of terraces [241] and interference patterns due to defects at or below the graphene layers [342].

II.5 Graphene stacks

In stacks with more than one graphene layer, two consecutive layers are normally oriented in such a way that the atoms in one of the two sublattices, AnA_{n}, of the honeycomb structure of one layer are directly above one half of the atoms in the neighboring layer, sublattice An±1A_{n\pm 1}. The second set of atoms in one layer sits on top of the (empty) center of an hexagon in the other layer. The shortest distance between carbon atoms in different layers is dAn​An±1=c=3.4d_{A_{n}A_{n\pm 1}}=c=3.4Å. The next distance is dAn​Bn±1=c2+a2d_{A_{n}B_{n\pm 1}}=\sqrt{c^{2}+a^{2}}. This is the most common arrangement of nearest neighbor layers observed in nature, although a stacking order in which all atoms in one layer occupy positions directly above the atoms in the neighboring layers (hexagonal stacking) has been considered theoretically [80] and appears in graphite intercalated compounds [106].

The relative position of two neighboring layers allows for two different orientations of the third layer. If we label the positions of the two first atoms as 1 and 2, the third layer can be of type 1, leading to the sequence 121, or it can fill a third position different from 1 and 2 (see Fig. 12), labeled 3. There are no more inequivalent positions where a new layer can be placed, so that thicker stacks can be described in terms of these three orientations. In the most common version of bulk graphite the stacking order is 1212⋯1212\cdots (Bernal stacking). Regions with the stacking 123123⋯123123\cdots (rhombohedral stacking) have also been observed in different types of graphite [30, 132]. Finally, samples with no discernible stacking order (turbostratic graphite) are also commonly reported.

Beyond two layers, the stack ordering can be arbitrarily complex. Simple analytical expressions for the electronic bands can be obtained for perfect Bernal ( 1212⋯1212\cdots ) and rhombohedral ( 123123⋯123123\cdots ) stacking [154]. Even if we consider one interlayer hopping, t⟂=γ1t_{\perp}=\gamma_{1}, the two stacking orders show rather different band structures near ϵ=0\epsilon=0. A Bernal stack with NN layers, NN even, has N/2N/2 electron like and N/2N/2 hole like parabolic subbands touching at ϵ=0\epsilon=0. When NN is odd, an additional subband with linear (Dirac) dispersion emerges. Rhombohedral systems have only two subbands that touch at ϵ=0\epsilon=0. These subbands disperse as kNk^{N}, and become surface states localized at the top and bottom layer when N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. In this limit, the remaining 2​N−22N-2 subbands of a rhombohedral stack become Dirac like, with the same Fermi velocity as a single graphene layer. The subband structure of a tri-layer with the Bernal stacking includes two touching parabolic bands, and one with Dirac dispersion, combining the features of bilayer and monolayer graphene.

The low energy bands have different weights on the two sublattices of each graphene layer. The states at a site directly coupled to the neighboring planes are pushed to energies ϵ≈±t⟂\epsilon\approx\pm t_{\perp}. The bands near ϵ=0\epsilon=0 are localized mostly at the sites without neighbors in the next layers. For the Bernal stacking, this feature implies that the density of states at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 at sites without nearest neighbors in the contiguous layers is finite, while it vanishes linearly at the other sites. In stacks with rhombohedral stacking, all sites have one neighbor in another plane, and the density of states vanishes at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 [154]. This result is consistent with the well known fact that only one of the two sublattices at a graphite surface can be resolved by scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) [404].

As in the case of a bilayer, an inhomogeneous charge distribution can change the electrostatic potential in the different layers. For more than two layers, this breaking of the equivalence between layers can take place even in the absence of an applied electric field. It is interesting to note that a gap can open in a stack with Bernal ordering and four layers, if the electronic charge at the two surface layers is different from that at the two inner ones. Systems with a higher number of layers do not show a gap, even in the presence of charge inhomogeneity. Four representative examples are shown in Fig. 13. The band structure analyzed here will be modified by the inclusion of the trigonal warping term, γ3\gamma_{3}. Experimental studies of graphene stacks have showed that, with increasing number of layers, the system becomes increasingly metallic (concentration of charge carriers at zero energy gradually increases), and there appear several types of electron-and-hole-like carries [293, 268]. An inhomogeneous charge distribution between layers becomes very important in this case, leading to 2D electron and hole systems that occupy only a few graphene layers near the surface and can completely dominate transport properties of graphene stacks [268].

The degeneracies of the bands at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 can be studied using topological arguments [238]. Multilayers with an even number of layers and Bernal stacking have inversion symmetry, leading to degeneracies with winding number +2, as in the case of a bilayer. The trigonal lattice symmetry implies that these points can lead, at most, to four Dirac points. In stacks with an odd number of layers, these degeneracies can be completely removed. The winding number of the degeneracies found in stacks with NN layers and orthorhombic ordering is ±N\pm N. The inclusion of trigonal warping terms will lead to the existence of many weaker degeneracies near ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Furthermore, it is well known that in graphite the planes can be rotated relative each other giving rise to Moiré patterns that are observed in STM of graphite surfaces [338]. The graphene layers can be rotated relative to each other due to the weak coupling between planes that allows for the presence of many different orientational states that are quasidegenerate in energy. For certain angles the graphene layers become commensurate with each other leading to a lowering of the electronic energy. Such phenomenon is quite similar to the commensurate-incommensurate transitions observed in certain charge density wave systems or adsorption of gases on graphite [32]. This kind of dependence of the electronic structure on the relative rotation angle between graphene layers leads to what is called super-lubricity in graphite [100], namely, the vanishing of the friction between layers as a function of the angle of rotation. In the case of bilayer graphene, a rotation by a small commensurate angle leads to the effective decoupling between layers and the recovery of the linear Dirac spectrum of the single layer albeit with a modification on the value of the Fermi velocity [232].

II.5.1 Electronic structure of bulk graphite

The tight-binding description of graphene described earlier can be extended to systems with an infinite number of layers. The coupling between layers leads to hopping terms between π\pi orbitals in different layers, leading to the so called Slonczewski-Weiss-McClure model [378]. This model describes the band structure of bulk graphite with the Bernal stacking order in terms of seven parameters, γ0,γ1,γ2,γ3,γ4,γ5\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4},\gamma_{5} and Δ\Delta. The parameter γ0\gamma_{0} describes the hopping within each layer, and it has been considered previously. The coupling between orbitals in atoms that are nearest neighbors in successive layers is γ1\gamma_{1}, which we called t⟂t_{\perp} earlier. The parameters γ3\gamma_{3} and γ4\gamma_{4} describe the hopping between orbitals at next nearest neighbors in successive layers and were discussed in the case of the bilayer. The coupling between orbitals at next nearest neighbor layers are γ2\gamma_{2} and γ5\gamma_{5}. Finally, Δ\Delta is an on site energy which reflects the inequivalence between the two sublattices in each graphene layer once the presence of neighboring layers is taken into account. The values of these parameters, and their dependence with pressure, or, equivalently, the interatomic distances, have been extensively studied [255, 297, 385, 258, 108, 101, 56]. A representative set of values is shown in Table[1]. It is unknown, however, how these parameters may vary in graphene stacks with a small number of layers.

The unit cell of graphite with Bernal stacking includes two layers, and two atoms within each layer. The tight-binding Hamiltonian described previously can be represented as a 4×44\times 4 matrix. In the continuum limit, the two inequivalent corners of the BZ can be treated separately, and the in plane terms can be described by the Dirac equation. The next terms in importance for the low energy electronic spectrum are the nearest neighbor couplings γ1\gamma_{1} and γ3\gamma_{3}. The influence of the parameter γ4\gamma_{4} on the low energy bands is much smaller, as discussed below. Finally, the fine details of the spectrum of bulk graphite are determined by Δ\Delta, which breaks the electron-hole symmetry of the bands preserved by γ0,γ1\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1} and γ3\gamma_{3}. It is usually assumed to be much smaller than the other terms.

We label the two atoms from the unit cell in one layer as 1 and 2, and 3 and 4 correspond to the second layer. Atoms 2 and 3 are directly on top of each other. Then, the matrix elements of the Hamiltonian can be written as:

H11K\displaystyle H_{11}^{K} =\displaystyle= 2​γ2​cos⁡(2​π​kz/c)\displaystyle 2\gamma_{2}\cos(2\pi k_{z}/c)
H12K\displaystyle H_{12}^{K} =\displaystyle= vF​(kx+i​ky)\displaystyle v_{F}(k_{x}+ik_{y})
H13K\displaystyle H_{13}^{K} =\displaystyle= 3​γ4​a2​(1+ei​kz​c)​(kx+i​ky)\displaystyle\frac{3\gamma_{4}a}{2}\left(1+e^{ik_{z}c}\right)\left(k_{x}+ik_{y}\right)
H14K\displaystyle H_{14}^{K} =\displaystyle= 3​γ3​a2​(1+ei​kz​c)​(kx−i​ky)\displaystyle\frac{3\gamma_{3}a}{2}\left(1+e^{ik_{z}c}\right)\left(k_{x}-ik_{y}\right)
H22K\displaystyle H_{22}^{K} =\displaystyle= Δ+2​γ5​cos⁡(2​π​kz/c)\displaystyle\Delta+2\gamma_{5}\cos(2\pi k_{z}/c)
H23K\displaystyle H_{23}^{K} =\displaystyle= γ1​(1+ei​kz​c)\displaystyle\gamma_{1}\left(1+e^{ik_{z}c}\right)
H24K\displaystyle H_{24}^{K} =\displaystyle= 3​γ4​a2​(1+ei​kz​c)​(kx+i​ky)\displaystyle\frac{3\gamma_{4}a}{2}\left(1+e^{ik_{z}c}\right)\left(k_{x}+ik_{y}\right)
H33K\displaystyle H_{33}^{K} =\displaystyle= Δ+2​γ5​cos⁡(2​π​kz/c)\displaystyle\Delta+2\gamma_{5}\cos(2\pi k_{z}/c)
H34K\displaystyle H_{34}^{K} =\displaystyle= vF​(kx+i​ky)\displaystyle v_{F}(k_{x}+ik_{y})
H44K\displaystyle H_{44}^{K} =\displaystyle= 2​γ2​cos⁡(2​π​kz/c)\displaystyle 2\gamma_{2}\cos(2\pi k_{z}/c) (63)

where cc is the lattice constant in the out of plane direction, equal to twice the interlayer spacing. The matrix elements of HK′H^{K^{\prime}} can be obtained by replacing kxk_{x} by −kx-k_{x} (other conventions for the unit cell and the orientation of the lattice lead to different phases). Recent ARPES experiments [445, 302, 448, 54] performed in epitaxially grown graphene stacks [42] confirm the main features of this model, formulated mainly on the basis of Fermi surface measurements [255, 385]. The electronic spectrum of the model can also be calculated in a magnetic field [135, 275], and the results are also consistent with STM on graphite surfaces [249, 205, 279, 230], epitaxially grown graphene stacks [241], and with optical measurements in the infrared range [231].

II.6 Surface states in graphene

So far, we have discussed the basic bulk properties of graphene. Nevertheless, graphene has very interesting surface (edge) states that do not occur in other systems. A semi-infinite graphene sheet with a zigzag edge has a band of zero energy states localized at the surface [130, 420, 273]. In section II.8 we will discuss the existence of edge states using the Dirac equation. Here will discuss the same problem using the tight-binding Hamiltonian. To see why these edge states exist we consider the ribbon geometry with zigzag edges shown in Fig. 14. The ribbon width is such that it has NN unit cells in the transverse cross section (yy direction). We will assume that the ribbon has infinite length in the longitudinal direction (xx direction).

Let us rewrite (5), with t′=0t^{\prime}=0, in terms of the integer indices mm and nn, introduced in Fig. 14, and labeling the unit cells:

H\displaystyle H =\displaystyle= −t∑m,n,σ[aσ†(m,n)bσ(m,n)+aσ†(m,n)bσ(m−1,n)\displaystyle-t\sum_{m,n,\sigma}[a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m,n)+a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m-1,n) (64)
+aσ†(m,n)bσ(m,n−1)+h.c.].\displaystyle+a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m,n-1)+\textrm{h.c.}].

Given that the ribbon is infinite in the 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} direction one can introduce a Fourier decomposition of the operators leading to

The solution of the Schrödinger equation, H1​p|μ,k,σ⟩=Eμ,k|μ,k,σ⟩H^{1p}\left|\mu,k,\sigma\right\rangle=E_{\mu,k}\left|\mu,k,\sigma\right\rangle, can be generally expressed as:

|μ,k,σ⟩=∑n[α(k,n)|a,k,n,σ⟩+β(k,n)|b,k,n,σ⟩],\left|\mu,k,\sigma\right\rangle=\sum_{n}[\alpha(k,n)\left|a,k,n,\sigma\right\rangle+\beta(k,n)\left|b,k,n,\sigma\right\rangle], (67)

Let us consider, for simplicity, a semi-infinite system with a single edge. We must require the convergence condition |−2​cos⁡(k​a/2)|<1\left|-2\cos(ka/2)\right|<1, in (77) because otherwise the wavefunction would diverge in the semi-infinite graphene sheet. Therefore, the semi-infinite system has edge states for k​aka in the region 2​π/3<k​a<4​π/32\pi/3<ka<4\pi/3, which corresponds to 1/31/3 of the possible momenta. Note that the amplitudes of the edge states are given by,

|α⁡(k,n)|\displaystyle|\alpha(k,n)| =\displaystyle= 2λ⁡(k)e−n/λ(k),\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda(k)}}e^{-n/\lambda(k)}, (78)
|β⁡(k,n)|\displaystyle|\beta(k,n)| =\displaystyle= 2λ⁡(k)e−(N−1−n)/λ(k),\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda(k)}}e^{-(N-1-n)/\lambda(k)}, (79)

where the penetration length is given by:

λ(k)=−1/ln|2cos(ka/2)|.\displaystyle\lambda(k)=-1/\ln|2\cos(ka/2)|. (80)

It is easily seen that the penetration length diverges when k​aka approaches the limits of the region ]2​π/3,4​π/3[]2\pi/3,4\pi/3[.

Although the boundary conditions defined by Eqs. (74) and (75) are satisfied for solutions (76) and (77) in the semi-infinite system, they are not in the ribbon geometry. In fact, Eqs. (78) and (79) are eigenstates only in the semi-infinite system. In the graphene ribbon the two edge states, which come from both sides of the edge, will overlap with each other. The bonding and anti-bonding states formed by the two edge states will then be the ribbon eigenstates [420] (note that at zero energy there are no other states with which the edge states could hybridize). As bonding and anti-bonding states result in a gap in energy the zero energy flat bands of edge states will become slightly dispersive, depending on the ribbon width NN. The overlap between the two edge states is larger as k​aka approaches 2​π/32\pi/3 and 4​π/34\pi/3. This means that deviations from zero energy flatness will be stronger near these points.

Edge states in graphene nanoribbons, just as the case of carbon nanotubes, are predicted to be Luttinger liquids, that is, interacting one-dimensional electron systems [75]. Hence, clean nanoribbons must have 1D square root singularities in their density of states [273] that can be probed by Raman spectroscopy. Disorder may smooth out these singularities, however. In the presence of a magnetic field, when the bulk states are gapped, the edge states are responsible for the transport of spin and charge [1, 2, 4, 3].

II.7 Surface states in graphene stacks

Single layer graphene can be considered a zero gap semiconductor, which leads to the extensively studied possibility of gap states, at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, as discussed in the previous section. The most studied such states are those localized near a graphene zigzag edge [130, 421]. It can be shown analytically [71] that a bilayer zigzag edge, like that shown in Fig. 15, analyzed within the nearest neighbor tight-binding approximation described before, has two bands of localized states, one completely localized in the top layer and indistinguishable from similar states in single layer graphene, and another band which alternates between the two layers. These states, as they lie at ϵ=0\epsilon=0, have finite amplitudes on one half of the sites only.

These bands, as in single layer graphene, occupy one third of the BZ of a stripe bounded by zigzag edges. They become dispersive in a biased bilayer. As graphite can be described in terms of effective bilayer systems, one for each value of the perpendicular momentum, kzk_{z}, bulk graphite with a zigzag termination should show one surface band per layer.

II.8 The spectrum of graphene nanoribbons

The spectrum of graphene nanoribbons depend very much on the nature of their edges – zigzag or armchair [57, 58, 273]. In Fig. 16 we show a honeycomb lattice having zigzag edges along the xx direction and armchair edges along the yy direction. If we choose the ribbon to be infinite in the xx direction we produce a graphene nanoribbon with zigzag edges; conversely choosing the ribbon to be macroscopically large along the yy but finite in the xx direction we produce a graphene nanoribbon with armchair edges.

In Fig. 17 we show the fourteen energy levels, calculated in the tight-binding approximation, closest to zero energy for a nanoribbon with zigzag and armchair edges and of width N=200N=200 unit cells. We can see that they are both metallic, and that the zigzag ribbon presents a band of zero energy modes that is absent in the armchair case. This band at zero energy is the surface states living near the edge of the graphene ribbon. More detailed ab initio calculations of the spectra of graphene nanoribbons show that interaction effects can lead to electronic gaps [383] and magnetic states close to the graphene edges, independent of their nature [382, 436, 435].

From the experimental point of view, however, graphene nanoribbons currently have a high degree of roughness at the edges. Such edge disorder can change significantly the properties of edge states [28, 157], leading to Anderson localization, and anomalies in the quantum Hall effect [75, 246] as well as Coulomb blockade effects [380]. Such effects have already been observed in lithographically engineered graphene nanoribbons [163, 309]. Furthermore, the problem of edge passivation by hydrogen or other elements is not clearly understood experimentally at this time. Passivation can be modeled in the tight-binding approach by modifications of the hopping energies [291] or via additional phases in the boundary conditions [190]. Theoretical modeling of edge passivation indicate that those have a strong effect on the electronic properties at the edge of graphene nanoribbons [37, 177].

In what follows we derive the spectrum for both zigzag and armchair edges directly from the Dirac equation. This was originally done both with and without a magnetic field [57, 58, 273].

II.8.1 Zigzag nanoribbons

In the geometry of Fig. 16 the unit cell vectors are 𝒂1=a0​(1,0)\bm{a}_{1}=a_{0}(1,0) and 𝒂2=a0​(1/2,3/2)\bm{a}_{2}=a_{0}\left(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2\right), which generate the unit vectors of the BZ given by 𝒃1=4π/(a03)(3/2,−1/2)\bm{b}_{1}=4\pi/(a_{0}\sqrt{3})\left(\sqrt{3}/2,-1/2\right) and 𝒃2=4​π/(a0​3)​(0,1)\bm{b}_{2}=4\pi/(a_{0}\sqrt{3})(0,1). From these two vectors we find two inequivalent Dirac points given by 𝑲=(4​π/3​a0,0)=(K,0)\bm{K}=\left(4\pi/3a_{0},0\right)=(K,0) and 𝑲′=(−4π/3a0,0)=(−K,0)\bm{K}^{\prime}=\left(-4\pi/3a_{0},0\right)=(-K,0), with a0=3​aa_{0}=\sqrt{3}a. The Dirac Hamiltonian around the Dirac point 𝑲\bm{K} reads in momentum space:

H𝑲=vF​(0px−i​pypx+i​py0),H_{\bm{K}}=v_{F}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&p_{x}-ip_{y}\\ p_{x}+ip_{y}&0\end{array}\right), (81)

and around the 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} as:

H𝑲′=vF​(0px+i​pypx−i​py0).H_{\bm{K}^{\prime}}=v_{F}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&p_{x}+ip_{y}\\ p_{x}-ip_{y}&0\end{array}\right). (82)

The wavefunction, in real space, for the sublattice AA is given by:

ΨA​(𝒓)=ei​𝑲⋅𝒓​ψA​(𝒓)+ei​𝑲′⋅𝒓​ψA′​(𝒓),\Psi_{A}(\bm{r})=e^{i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi_{A}(\bm{r})+e^{i\bm{K}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi^{\prime}_{A}(\bm{r})\,, (83)

and for sublattice BB is given by

ΨB​(𝒓)=ei​𝑲⋅𝒓​ψB​(𝒓)+ei​𝑲′⋅𝒓​ψB′​(𝒓),\Psi_{B}(\bm{r})=e^{i\bm{K}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi_{B}(\bm{r})+e^{i\bm{K}^{\prime}\cdot\bm{r}}\psi^{\prime}_{B}(\bm{r})\,, (84)

where ψA\psi_{A} and ψB\psi_{B} are the components of the spinor wavefunction of Hamiltonian (81) and ψA′\psi^{\prime}_{A} and ψB′\psi^{\prime}_{B} have identical meaning but relatively to (82). Let us assume that the edges of the nanoribbons are parallel to the x−x-axis. In this case, the translational symmetry guarantees that the spinor wavefunction can be written as:

ψ⁡(𝒓)=ei​kx​x​(ϕA​(y)ϕB​(y)),\psi(\bm{r})=e^{ik_{x}x}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\phi_{A}(y)\\ \phi_{B}(y)\end{array}\right), (85)

and a similar equation for the spinor of Hamiltonian (82). For zigzag edges the boundary conditions at the edge of the ribbon (located at y=0y=0 and y=Ly=L, where LL is the ribbon width) are:

ΨA​(y=L)=0,ΨB​(y=0)=0,\Psi_{A}(y=L)=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\Psi_{B}(y=0)=0\,, (86)

leading to:

0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​K​x​ei​kx​x​ϕA​(L)+e−i​K​x​ei​kx​x​ϕA′​(L),\displaystyle e^{iKx}e^{ik_{x}x}\phi_{A}(L)+e^{-iKx}e^{ik_{x}x}\phi^{\prime}_{A}(L)\,, (87)
0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​K​x​ei​kx​x​ϕB​(0)+e−i​K​x​ei​kx​x​ϕB′​(0).\displaystyle e^{iKx}e^{ik_{x}x}\phi_{B}(0)+e^{-iKx}e^{ik_{x}x}\phi^{\prime}_{B}(0)\,. (88)

The boundary conditions (87) and (88) are satisfied for any xx by the choice:

ϕA​(L)=ϕA′​(L)=ϕB​(0)=ϕB′​(0)=0.\phi_{A}(L)=\phi^{\prime}_{A}(L)=\phi_{B}(0)=\phi^{\prime}_{B}(0)=0\,. (89)

We need now to find out the form of the envelope functions. The eigenfunction around the point 𝐊{\bf K} has the form:

(0kx−∂ykx+∂y0)​(ϕA​(y)ϕB​(y))=ϵ~​(ϕA​(y)ϕB​(y)),\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&k_{x}-\partial_{y}\\ k_{x}+\partial_{y}&0\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\phi_{A}(y)\\ \phi_{B}(y)\end{array}\right)=\tilde{\epsilon}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\phi_{A}(y)\\ \phi_{B}(y)\end{array}\right), (90)

with ϵ~=ϵ/vF\tilde{\epsilon}=\epsilon/v_{F} and ϵ\epsilon the energy eigenvalue. The eigenproblem can be written as two linear differential equations of the form:

{(kx−∂y)ϕB=ϵ~ϕA,(kx+∂y)ϕA=ϵ~ϕB.\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}(k_{x}-\partial_{y})\phi_{B}=\tilde{\epsilon}\phi_{A}\,,\\ (k_{x}+\partial_{y})\phi_{A}=\tilde{\epsilon}\phi_{B}.\end{array}\right. (91)

Applying the operator (kx+∂y)(k_{x}+\partial_{y}) to the first of Eqs. (91) leads to:

(−∂y2+kx2)ϕB=ϵ~2ϕB,(-\partial^{2}_{y}+k_{x}^{2})\phi_{B}=\tilde{\epsilon}^{2}\phi_{B}, (92)

with ϕA\phi_{A} given by:

ϕA=1ϵ~(kx−∂y)ϕB.\phi_{A}=\frac{1}{\tilde{\epsilon}}(k_{x}-\partial_{y})\phi_{B}\,. (93)

The solution of (92) has the form:

ϕB=A​ez​y+B​e−z​y,\phi_{B}=Ae^{zy}+Be^{-zy}, (94)

leading to an eigenenergy ϵ~2=kx2−z2\tilde{\epsilon}^{2}=k^{2}_{x}-z^{2}. The boundary conditions for a zigzag edge require that ϕA​(y=L)=0\phi_{A}(y=L)=0 and ϕB​(y=0)=0\phi_{B}(y=0)=0, leading to:

{ϕB​(y=0)=0⇔A+B=0,ϕA​(y=L)=0⇔(kx−z)​A​ez​L+(kx+z)​B​e−z​L=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\phi_{B}(y=0)=0\Leftrightarrow A+B=0\,,\\ \phi_{A}(y=L)=0\Leftrightarrow(k_{x}-z)Ae^{zL}+(k_{x}+z)Be^{-zL}=0\end{array}\right., (95)

which leads to an eigenvalue equation of the form:

e−2​z​L=kx−zkx+z.e^{-2zL}=\frac{k_{x}-z}{k_{x}+z}\,. (96)

Equation (96) has real solutions for zz, whenever kxk_{x} is positive; these solutions correspond to surface waves (edge states) existing near the edge of the graphene ribbon. In section II.6 we discussed these states from the point of view of the tight-binding model. In addition to real solutions for zz, (96) also supports complex ones, of the form z=i​knz=ik_{n}, leading to:

kx=kntan⁡(kn​L).k_{x}=\frac{k_{n}}{\tan(k_{n}L)}. (97)

The solutions of (97) correspond to confined modes in the graphene ribbon.

If we apply the same procedure to the Dirac equation around the Dirac point 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} we obtain a different eigenvalue equation given by:

e−2​z​L=kx+zkx−z.e^{-2zL}=\frac{k_{x}+z}{k_{x}-z}\,. (98)

This equation supports real solutions for zz if kxk_{x} is negative. Therefore we have edge states for negative values kxk_{x}, with momentum around 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime}. As in the case of 𝑲\bm{K}, the system also supports confined modes, given by:

kx=−kntan⁡(kn​L).k_{x}=-\frac{k_{n}}{\tan(k_{n}L)}. (99)

One should note that the eigenvalue equations for 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} are obtained from those for 𝑲\bm{K} by inversion, kx→−kxk_{x}\rightarrow-k_{x}.

We finally notice that the edge states for zigzag nanoribbons are dispersionless (localized in real space) when t′=0t^{\prime}=0. When electron-hole symmetry is broken (t′≠0t^{\prime}\neq 0) these states become dispersive with a Fermi velocity ve≈t′​av_{e}\approx t^{\prime}a [75].

II.8.2 Armchair nanoribbons

Let us now consider an armchair nanoribbon with armchair edges along the yy direction. The boundary conditions at the edges of the ribbon (located at x=0x=0 and x=Lx=L, where LL is the width of the ribbon):

ΨA​(x=0)=ΨB​(x=0)=ΨA​(x=L)=ΨB​(x=L)=0.\Psi_{A}(x=0)=\Psi_{B}(x=0)=\Psi_{A}(x=L)=\Psi_{B}(x=L)=0\,. (100)

Translational symmetry guarantees that the spinor wavefunction of Hamiltonian (81) can be written as:

ψ⁡(𝒓)=ei​ky​y​(ϕA​(x)ϕB​(x)),\psi(\bm{r})=e^{ik_{y}y}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\phi_{A}(x)\\ \phi_{B}(x)\end{array}\right), (101)

and a similar equation for the spinor of the Hamiltonian (82). The boundary conditions have the form:

0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​ky​y​ϕA​(0)+ei​ky​y​ϕA′​(0),\displaystyle e^{ik_{y}y}\phi_{A}(0)+e^{ik_{y}y}\phi^{\prime}_{A}(0)\,, (102)
0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​ky​y​ϕB​(0)+ei​ky​y​ϕB′​(0),\displaystyle e^{ik_{y}y}\phi_{B}(0)+e^{ik_{y}y}\phi^{\prime}_{B}(0)\,, (103)
0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​K​L​ei​ky​y​ϕA​(L)+e−i​K​L​ei​ky​y​ϕA′​(L),\displaystyle e^{iKL}e^{ik_{y}y}\phi_{A}(L)+e^{-iKL}e^{ik_{y}y}\phi^{\prime}_{A}(L)\,, (104)
0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= ei​K​L​ei​ky​y​ϕB​(L)+e−i​K​L​ei​ky​y​ϕB′​(L),\displaystyle e^{iKL}e^{ik_{y}y}\phi_{B}(L)+e^{-iKL}e^{ik_{y}y}\phi^{\prime}_{B}(L)\,, (105)

and are satisfied for any yy if:

ϕμ​(0)+ϕμ′​(0)=0,\phi_{\mu}(0)+\phi^{\prime}_{\mu}(0)=0\,, (106)

and

ei​K​L​ϕμ​(L)+e−i​K​L​ϕμ′​(L)=0,e^{iKL}\phi_{\mu}(L)+e^{-iKL}\phi^{\prime}_{\mu}(L)=0\,, (107)

with μ=A,B\mu=A,B. It is clear that these boundary conditions mix states from the two Dirac points. Now we must find the form of the envelope functions obeying the boundary conditions (106) and (107). As before, the functions ϕB\phi_{B} and ϕB′\phi^{\prime}_{B} obey the second order differential equation (92) (with yy replaced by xx) and the function ϕA\phi_{A} and ϕA′\phi^{\prime}_{A} are determined from (93). The solutions of (92) have the form:

ϕB\displaystyle\phi_{B} =\displaystyle= A​ei​kn​x+B​e−i​kn​x,\displaystyle Ae^{ik_{n}x}+Be^{-ik_{n}x}\,, (108)
ϕB′\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}_{B} =\displaystyle= C​ei​kn​x+D​e−i​kn​x.\displaystyle Ce^{ik_{n}x}+De^{-ik_{n}x}\,. (109)

Applying the boundary conditions: (106) and (107), one obtains:

0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= A+B+C+D,\displaystyle A+B+C+D\,, (110)
0\displaystyle 0 =\displaystyle= A​ei⁡(kn+K)​L+D​e−i⁡(kn+K)​L\displaystyle Ae^{i(k_{n}+K)L}+De^{-i(k_{n}+K)L} (111)
+\displaystyle+ B​e−i⁡(kn−K)​L+C​ei⁡(kn−K)​L.\displaystyle Be^{-i(k_{n}-K)L}+Ce^{i(k_{n}-K)L}\,.

The boundary conditions are satisfied with the choice:

A=−D,B=C=0,A=-D\,,\hskip 28.45274ptB=C=0\,, (112)

which leads to sin⁡[(kn+K)​L]=0\sin[(k_{n}+K)L]=0. Therefore the allowed values of knk_{n} are given by

kn=n​πL−4​π3​a0,k_{n}=\frac{n\pi}{L}-\frac{4\pi}{3a_{0}}\,, (113)

and the eigenenergies are given by:

ϵ~2=ky2+kn2.\tilde{\epsilon}^{2}=k^{2}_{y}+k^{2}_{n}\,. (114)

No surface states exist in this case.

II.9 Dirac fermions in a magnetic field

Let us now consider the problem of a uniform magnetic field BB applied perpendicular to the graphene plane 22 2 The problem of transverse magnetic and electric fields can also be solved exactly. See: [235, 318].. We use the Landau gauge: 𝐀=B⁡(−y,0){\bf A}=B(-y,0). Notice that the magnetic field introduces a new length scale in the problem:

ℓB=ce​B,\displaystyle\ell_{B}=\sqrt{\frac{c}{eB}}\,, (115)

which is the magnetic length. The only other scale in the problem is the Fermi-Dirac velocity. Dimensional analysis shows that the only quantity with dimensions of energy we can make is vF/ℓBv_{F}/\ell_{B}. In fact, this determines the cyclotron frequency of the Dirac fermions:

ωc=2​vFℓB\displaystyle\omega_{c}=\sqrt{2}\,\frac{v_{F}}{\ell_{B}} (116)

(the 2\sqrt{2} factor comes from the quantization of the problem, see below). Eqs. (116) and (115) show that the cyclotron energy scales like B\sqrt{B}, in clear contrast with the non-relativistic problem where the cyclotron energy is linear in BB. This implies that the energy scale associated with the Dirac fermions is rather different from the one find in the ordinary 2D electron gas. For instance, for fields of the order B≈10B\approx 10 T the cyclotron energy in the 2D electron gas is of the order of 10 K. In contrast, for the Dirac fermion problem, for the same fields, the cyclotron energy is of the order of 1,0001,000 K, that is, two orders of magnitude bigger. This has strong implications for the observation of the quantum Hall effect at room temperature [295]. Furthermore, for B=10B=10 T the Zeeman energy is relatively small, g​μB​B≈5g\mu_{B}B\approx 5 K, and can be disregarded.

Let us now consider the Dirac equation in more detail. Using the minimal coupling in (29) (i.e., replacing −i∇-i\nabla by −i∇+e𝐀/c-i\nabla+e{\bf A}/c) we find:

vF[σ→⋅(−i∇+e𝐀/c)]ψ(𝐫)\displaystyle v_{F}\left[\vec{\sigma}\cdot(-i\nabla+e{\bf A}/c)\right]\psi({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= E​ψ​(𝐫),\displaystyle E\,\,\psi({\bf r})\,, (117)

in the Landau gauge the generic solution for the wavefunction has the form ψ⁡(x,y)=ei​k​x​ϕ​(y)\psi(x,y)=e^{ikx}\phi(y), and the Dirac equation reads:

vF​[0∂y−k+Bey/c−∂y−k+Bey/c0]​ϕ​(y)\displaystyle v_{F}\!\left[\!\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\partial_{y}\!-\!k\!+\!Bey/c\\ -\partial_{y}\!-\!k\!+\!Bey/c&0\end{array}\!\right]\!\phi(y)\!\! =\displaystyle= E​ϕ​(y),\displaystyle\!\!E\phi(y)\,,

that can be rewritten as:

ωc​[0𝒪𝒪†0]​ϕ​(ξ)=E​ϕ​(ξ),\displaystyle\omega_{c}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}0&{\cal O}\\ {\cal O}^{{\dagger}}&0\end{array}\right]\phi(\xi)=E\,\phi(\xi)\,,

or equivalently:

(𝒪​σ++𝒪†​σ−)​ϕ=(2​E/ωc)​ϕ,\displaystyle({\cal O}\sigma^{+}+{\cal O}^{{\dagger}}\sigma^{-})\phi=(2E/\omega_{c})\phi\,, (124)

where σ±=σx±i​σy\sigma^{\pm}=\sigma_{x}\pm i\sigma_{y}, and we have defined the dimensionless length scale:

ξ\displaystyle\xi =\displaystyle= yℓB−ℓB​k,\displaystyle\frac{y}{\ell_{B}}-\ell_{B}k\,, (125)

and 1D harmonic oscillator operators:

𝒪\displaystyle{\cal O} =\displaystyle= 12(∂ξ+ξ),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\partial_{\xi}+\xi\right)\,,
𝒪†\displaystyle{\cal O}^{{\dagger}} =\displaystyle= 12(−∂ξ+ξ),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(-\partial_{\xi}+\xi\right)\,, (126)

that obey canonical commutation relations: [𝒪,𝒪†]=1[{\cal O},{\cal O}^{{\dagger}}]=1. The number operator is simply: N=𝒪†​𝒪N={\cal O}^{{\dagger}}{\cal O}.

Firstly, we notice that (124) allows for a solution with zero energy:

(𝒪​σ++𝒪†​σ−)​ϕ0=0,\displaystyle({\cal O}\sigma^{+}+{\cal O}^{{\dagger}}\sigma^{-})\phi_{0}=0\,, (127)

and since the Hilbert space generated by σ→\vec{\sigma} is of dimension 22, and the spectrum generated by 𝒪†{\cal O}^{{\dagger}} is bounded from below, we just need to ensure that:

𝒪​ϕ0\displaystyle{\cal O}\phi_{0} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0\,,
σ−​ϕ0\displaystyle\sigma^{-}\phi_{0} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0\,, (128)

in order for (127) to be fulfilled. The obvious zero mode solution is:

ϕ0​(ξ)=ψ0​(ξ)⊗|⇓⟩,\displaystyle\phi_{0}(\xi)=\psi_{0}(\xi)\otimes|\Downarrow\rangle\,, (129)

where |⇓⟩|\Downarrow\rangle indicates the state localized on sublattice AA and |⇑⟩|\Uparrow\rangle indicates the state localized on sublattice BB. Furthermore,

𝒪​ψ0​(ξ)=0,\displaystyle{\cal O}\psi_{0}(\xi)=0\,, (130)

is the ground states of the 1D harmonic oscillator. All the solutions can now be constructed from the zero mode:

ϕN,±​(ξ)\displaystyle\phi_{N,\pm}(\xi) =\displaystyle= ψN−1​(ξ)⊗|⇑⟩±ψN​(ξ)⊗|⇓⟩\displaystyle\psi_{N-1}(\xi)\otimes|\Uparrow\rangle\pm\psi_{N}(\xi)\otimes|\Downarrow\rangle
=\displaystyle= (ψN−1​(ξ)±ψN​(ξ)),\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\psi_{N-1}(\xi)\\ \pm\psi_{N}(\xi)\end{array}\right)\,,

and their energy is given by [254]:

E±​(N)\displaystyle E_{\pm}(N) =\displaystyle= ±ωc​N,\displaystyle\pm\omega_{c}\sqrt{N}\,, (134)

where N=0,1,2,…N=0,1,2,... is a positive integer, ψN​(ξ)\psi_{N}(\xi) is the solution of the 1D Harmonic oscillator (explicitly: ψN(ξ)=2−N/2(N!)−1/2exp{−ξ2/2}HN(ξ)\psi_{N}(\xi)=2^{-N/2}(N!)^{-1/2}\exp\{-\xi^{2}/2\}H_{N}(\xi) where HN​(ξ)H_{N}(\xi) is a Hermite polynomial). The Landau levels at the opposite Dirac point, K’, have exactly the same spectrum and hence each Landau level is doubly degenerate. Of particular importance for the Dirac problem discussed here is the existence of a zero energy state N=0N=0 which is responsible, as we are going to show, to the anomalies observed in the quantum Hall effect. This particular Landau level structure has been observed by many different experimental probes, from Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in single layer graphene (see Fig. 18) [292, 443], to infrared spectroscopy [187], and to scanning tunneling spectroscopy [230] (STS) on a graphite surface.

II.10 The anomalous integer quantum Hall effect

In the presence of disorder Landau levels get broadened and mobility edges appear [220]. Notice that there will be a Landau level at zero energy that separates states with hole character (μ<0\mu<0) from states with electron character (μ>0\mu>0). The components of the resistivity and conductivity tensors are related by:

ρx​x\displaystyle\rho_{xx} =\displaystyle= σx​xσx​x2+σx​y2,\displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{xx}}{\sigma_{xx}^{2}+\sigma_{xy}^{2}}\,,
ρx​y\displaystyle\rho_{xy} =\displaystyle= σx​yσx​x2+σx​y2,\displaystyle\frac{\sigma_{xy}}{\sigma_{xx}^{2}+\sigma_{xy}^{2}}\,, (135)

where σx​x\sigma_{xx} (ρx​x\rho_{xx}) is the longitudinal component and σx​y\sigma_{xy} (ρx​y\rho_{xy}) is the Hall component of the conductivity (resistivity). When the chemical potential is inside of a region of localized states the longitudinal conductivity vanishes, σx​x=0\sigma_{xx}=0, and hence: ρx​x=0\rho_{xx}=0, ρx​y=1/σx​y\rho_{xy}=1/\sigma_{xy}.
