On the other hand, when the chemical potential is a region of delocalized states, when the chemical potential is crossing a Landau level, we have σx​x≠0\sigma_{xx}\neq 0 and σx​y\sigma_{xy} varies continuously [367, 368].

The value of σx​y\sigma_{xy} in the region of localized states can be obtained from Laughlin’s gauge invariance argument [220]: one imagines making a graphene ribbon such as the one in Fig. 19 with a magnetic field BB normal through its surface and a current II circling its loop. Due to the Lorentz force the magnetic field produces a Hall voltage VHV_{H} perpendicular to the field and current. The circulating current generates a magnetic flux Φ\Phi that threads the loop. The current is given by:

I=c​δ​Eδ​Φ,\displaystyle I=c\frac{\delta E}{\delta\Phi}\,, (136)

where EE is the total energy of the system. The localized states do not respond to changes in Φ\Phi, only the delocalized ones. When the flux is changed by a flux quantum δ​Φ=Φ0=h​c/e\delta\Phi=\Phi_{0}=hc/e the extended states remain the same by gauge invariance. If the chemical potential is in the region of localized states, all the extended states below the chemical potential will be filled both before and after the change of flux by Φ0\Phi_{0}. However, during the change of flux an integer number of states enter the cylinder at one edge and leave at the opposite edge.

The question is how many occupied states are transferred between edges. Let us consider a naive and as shown further incorrect calculation in order to show the importance of the zero mode in this problem. Each Landau level contributes with one state times its degeneracy gg. In the case of graphene we have g=4g=4 since there are 22 spin states and 22 Dirac cones. Hence, we would expect that when the flux changes by one flux quantum the change in energy would be δ​Einc.=±4​N​e​VH\delta E_{\rm inc.}=\pm 4NeV_{H}, where NN is an integer. The plus sign applies to electron states (charge +e+e) and the minus sign to hole states (charge −e-e). Hence, we would conclude that Iinc.=±4​(e2/h)​VHI_{\rm inc.}=\pm 4(e^{2}/h)V_{H} and hence σx​y,inc.=I/VH=±4Ne2/h\sigma_{xy,{\rm inc.}}=I/V_{H}=\pm 4Ne^{2}/h, which is the naive expectation. The problem with this result is that when the chemical potential is exactly at half-filling, that is, at the Dirac point, it would predict a Hall plateau at N=0N=0 with σx​y,inc.=0\sigma_{xy,{\rm inc.}}=0 which is not possible since there is a N=0N=0 Landau level, with extended states at this energy. The solution for this paradox is rather simple: because of the presence of the zero mode which is shared by the two Dirac points, there are exactly 2×(2​N+1)2\times(2N+1) occupied states that are transferred from one edge to another. Hence, the change in energy is δ​E=±2​(2​N+1)​e​VH\delta E=\pm 2(2N+1)eV_{H} for a change of flux of δ​Φ=h​c/e\delta\Phi=hc/e. Therefore, the Hall conductivity is [357, 322, 323, 160, 172]:

σx​y=IVH=cVH​δ​Eδ​Φ=±2​(2​N+1)​e2h,\displaystyle\sigma_{xy}=\frac{I}{V_{H}}=\frac{c}{V_{H}}\frac{\delta E}{\delta\Phi}=\pm 2(2N+1)\frac{e^{2}}{h}\,, (137)

without any Hall plateau at N=0N=0. This amazing result has been observed experimentally [292, 443] as shown in Fig.20.

II.11 Tight-binding model in a magnetic field

In the tight-binding approximation the hopping integrals are replaced by a Peierls substitution:

ei​e​∫𝐑𝐑′𝐀⋅d​𝐫​t𝐑,𝐑′=ei​2​πΦ0​∫𝐑𝐑′𝐀⋅d​𝐫​t𝐑,𝐑′,e^{ie\int_{\mathbf{R}}^{\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}\mathbf{A}\cdot\textrm{d}\mathbf{r}}t_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}=e^{i\frac{2\pi}{\Phi_{0}}\int_{\mathbf{R}}^{\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}\mathbf{A}\cdot\textrm{d}\mathbf{r}}t_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}}\,, (138)

where t𝐑,𝐑′t_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}} represents the hopping integral between the sites 𝐑\mathbf{R} and 𝐑′\mathbf{R}^{\prime}, with no field present. The tight-binding Hamiltonian for a single graphene layer, in a constant magnetic field perpendicular to the plane, is conveniently written as,

H=−t∑m,n,σ[ei​π​ΦΦ0​n​1+z2aσ†(m,n)bσ(m,n)+e−i​π​ΦΦ0​naσ†(m,n)bσ(m−1,n−(1−z)/2)+ei​π​ΦΦ0​n​z−12aσ†(m,n)bσ(m,n−z)+h.c.],H=-t\sum_{m,n,\sigma}[e^{i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n\frac{1+z}{2}}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m,n)+e^{-i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m-1,n-(1-z)/2)+e^{i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n\frac{z-1}{2}}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(m,n)b_{\sigma}(m,n-z)+\textrm{h.c.}], (139)

holding for a graphene stripe with a zigzag (z=1z=1) and armchair (z=−1z=-1) edges oriented along the x−x-direction. Fourier transforming along the xx direction gives,

H=−t∑k,n,σ[ei​π​ΦΦ0​n​1+z2aσ†(k,n)bσ(k,n)+e−i​π​ΦΦ0​nei​k​aaσ†(k,n)bσ(k,n−(1−z)/2)+ei​π​ΦΦ0​n​z−12aσ†(k,n)bσ(k,n−z)+h.c.].\displaystyle H=-t\sum_{k,n,\sigma}[e^{i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n\frac{1+z}{2}}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(k,n)b_{\sigma}(k,n)+e^{-i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n}e^{ika}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(k,n)b_{\sigma}(k,n-(1-z)/2)+e^{i\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n\frac{z-1}{2}}a_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(k,n)b_{\sigma}(k,n-z)+\textrm{h.c.}].

Let us now consider the case of zigzag edges. The eigenproblem can be rewritten in terms of Harper’s equations [164], and for zigzag edges we obtain [333]:

Eμ,k​α​(k,n)\displaystyle E_{\mu,k}\alpha(k,n) =\displaystyle= −t[ei​k​a/22cos(πΦΦ0n−k​a2)β(k,n)\displaystyle-t[e^{ika/2}2\cos(\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n-\frac{ka}{2})\beta(k,n) (140)
+\displaystyle+ β(k,n−1)],\displaystyle\beta(k,n-1)],
Eμ,k​β​(k,n)\displaystyle E_{\mu,k}\beta(k,n) =\displaystyle= −t[e−ika/22cos(πΦΦ0n−k​a2)α(k,n)\displaystyle-t[e^{-ika/2}2\cos(\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}n-\frac{ka}{2})\alpha(k,n) (141)
+\displaystyle+ α(k,n+1)],\displaystyle\alpha(k,n+1)],

where the coefficients α⁡(k,n)\alpha(k,n) and β⁡(k,n)\beta(k,n) show up in Hamiltonian’s eigenfunction, |ψ⁡(k)⟩|\psi(k)\rangle, written in terms of lattice-position-state states as:

|ψ(k)⟩=∑n,σ(α(k,n)|a;k,n,σ⟩+β(k,n)|b;k,n,σ⟩).|\psi(k)\rangle=\sum_{n,\sigma}\left(\alpha(k,n)|a;k,n,\sigma\rangle+\beta(k,n)|b;k,n,\sigma\rangle\right)\,. (142)

Eqs. (140) and (141) hold in the bulk. Considering that the zigzag ribbon has NN unit cells along its width, from n=0n=0 to n=N−1n=N-1, the boundary conditions at the edges are obtained from Eqs. (140) and (141), and read

Eμ,k​α​(k,0)=−t​ei​k​a/2​2​cos⁡(k​a2)​β​(k,0),\displaystyle E_{\mu,k}\alpha(k,0)=-te^{ika/2}2\cos\left(\frac{ka}{2}\right)\beta(k,0)\,, (143)
Eμ,kβ(k,N−)=−2te−ika/2cos[πΦΦ0(N−1)−k​a2]α(k,N−1).\displaystyle E_{\mu,k}\beta(k,N\!\!-\!\!1\!)\!\!=\!\!-2te^{-ika/2}\!\cos\!\left[\!\pi\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_{0}}(N\!\!-\!\!1)\!-\!\frac{ka}{2}\!\right]\!\alpha(k,N\!\!-\!\!1). (144)

Similar equations hold for a graphene ribbon with armchair edges.

In Fig. 21 we show fourteen energy levels, around zero energy, for both the zigzag and the armchair cases. The formation of the Landau levels is signaled by the presence of flat energy bands, following the bulk energy spectrum. From Fig. 21 it is straightforward to obtain the value of the Hall conductivity in the quantum Hall effect regime. Let us assume that the chemical potential is in between two Landau levels at positive energies, as represented by the dashed line in Fig. 21. The Landau level structure shows two zero energy modes, one of them is electron-like (hole-like), since close to the edge of the sample its energy is shifted upwards (downwards). The other Landau levels are doubly degenerate. The determination of the values for the Hall conductivity is done by counting how many energy levels (of electron-like nature) are below chemical potential. This counting produces the value (2​N+12N+1), with N=0,1,2,…N=0,1,2,\ldots (for the case of Fig. 21 one has N=2N=2). From this counting the Hall conductivity is given, including an extra factor of two accounting for the spin degree of freedom, by

σx​y=±2​e2h​(2​N+1)=±4​e2h​(N+12).\sigma_{xy}=\pm 2\frac{e^{2}}{h}(2N+1)=\pm 4\frac{e^{2}}{h}\left(N+\frac{1}{2}\right)\,. (145)

Eq. (145) leads to the anomalous integer quantum Hall effect discussed previously, which is the hallmark of single layer graphene.

II.12 Landau levels in graphene stacks

The dependence of the Landau level energies on the Landau index NN roughly follows the dispersion relation of the bands, as shown in Fig. 22. Note that, in a trilayer with Bernal stacking, two sets of levels have a N\sqrt{N} dependence, while the energies of other two depend linearly on NN. In an infinite rhombohedral stack, the Landau levels remain discrete and quasi-2D [154]. Note that, even in an infinite stack with the Bernal structure, the Landau level closest to E=0E=0 forms a band which does not overlap with the other Landau levels, leading to the possibility of a 3D integer quantum Hall effect [44, 211, 210, 236].

The optical transitions between Landau levels can also be calculated. The selection rules are the same as for a graphene single layer, and only transitions between subbands with Landau level indices MM and NN such that |N|=|M±1||N|=|M\pm 1| are allowed. The resulting transitions, with their respective spectral strengths, are shown in Fig. 23. The transitions are grouped into subbands, which give rise to a continuum when the number of layers tends to infinity. In Bernal stacks with an odd number of layers, the transitions associated to Dirac subbands with linear dispersion have the largest spectral strength, and they give a significant contribution to the total absorption even if the number of layers is large, NL≲30−40N_{\rm L}\lesssim 30-40 [347].

II.13 Diamagnetism

Back in 1952 Mrozowski [270] studied diamagnetism of polycrystalline graphite and other condensed-matter molecular-ring systems. It was concluded that in such ring systems diamagnetism has two contributions: (1) diamagnetism from the filled bands of electrons; (2) Landau diamagnetism of free electrons and holes. For graphite the second source of diamagnetism is by far the largest of the two.

McClure [254] computed diamagnetism of a 2D honeycomb lattice using the theory introduced by Wallace [422], a calculation he later generalized to three dimensional graphite [257]. For the honeycomb plane the magnetic susceptibility in units of emu/g is

χ=−0.0014T​γ02​sech2​(μ2​kB​T),\chi=-\frac{0.0014}{T}\gamma_{0}^{2}\,\mathrm{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{\mu}{2k_{B}T}\right)\,, (146)

where μ\mu is the Fermi energy, TT the temperature, and kBk_{B} the Boltzmann constant. For graphite the magnetic susceptibility is anisotropic and the difference between the susceptibility parallel to the principal axis and that perpendicular to the principal axis is -21.5×10−6\times 10^{-6} emu/g. The susceptibility perpendicular to the principal axis is about the free-atom susceptibility of -0.5×10−6\times 10^{-6} emu/g. In the 2D model the susceptibility turns out to be large due to the presence of fast moving electrons, with a velocity of the order of vF≃106v_{F}\simeq 10^{6} m/s, which in turn is a consequence of the large value of the hopping parameter γ0\gamma_{0}. In fact the susceptibility turns out to be proportional to the square of γ0\gamma_{0}. Later Sharma et al. extended the calculation of McClure for graphite by including the effect of trigonal warping and showed that the low temperature diamagnetism increases [365].

Safran and DiSalvo [349], interested in the susceptibility of graphite intercalation compounds, recalculated, in a tight-binding model, the susceptibility perpendicular to a graphite plane using Fukuyama’s theory [131], which includes interband transitions. The results agree with those published by McClure [254]. Later, Safran computed the susceptibility of a graphene bilayer showing that this system is diamagnetic at small values of the Fermi energy, but there appears a paramagnetic peak when the Fermi energy is of the order of the interlayer coupling [348].

The magnetic susceptibility of other carbon based materials, as carbon nanotubes and C60C_{60} molecular solids was measured [173] showing a diamagnetic response at finite magnetic fields different from that of graphite. The study of the magnetic response of nanographite ribbons with both zig-zag and arm-chair edges was done by Wakabayashi et al. using a numerical differentiation of the free energy [420]. From these two systems, the zig-zag edge state is of particular interest since the system supports edge states even in the presence of a magnetic field, leading to very high density of states near the edge of the ribbon. The high temperature response of these nanoribbons was found to be diamagnetic whereas the low temperature susceptibility is paramagnetic.

The Dirac-like nature of the electronic quasiparticles in graphene led [136] to consider in general the problem of the diamagnetism of nodal fermions and Nakamura to study the orbital magnetism of Dirac fermions in weak magnetic fields[274]. Koshino and Ando considered the diamagnetism of disordered graphene in the self consistent Born approximation, with a disorder potential of the form U⁡(𝒓)=𝟏​ui​δ​(𝒓−𝑹)U(\bm{r})=\bm{1}u_{i}\delta(\bm{r}-\bm{R}) [213]. At the neutrality point and zero temperature the susceptibility of disordered graphene is given by

χ⁡(0)=−gv​gs3​π2​e2​γ02​2​WΓ0,\chi(0)=-\frac{g_{v}g_{s}}{3\pi^{2}}\,e^{2}\gamma_{0}^{2}\,\frac{2W}{\Gamma_{0}}\,, (147)

where gs=gv=2g_{s}=g_{v}=2 is the spin and valley degeneracies, WW is a dimensionless parameter for the disorder strength, defined as W=ni​ui2/4​π​γ02W=n_{i}u^{2}_{i}/4\pi\gamma_{0}^{2}, nin_{i} the impurity concentration, and Γ0\Gamma_{0} is given by Γ0=ϵcexp[−1/(2W)]\Gamma_{0}=\epsilon_{c}\exp[-1/(2W)] with ϵc\epsilon_{c} a parameter defining a cut-off function used in the theory. At finite Fermi energy ϵF\epsilon_{F} and zero temperature the magnetic susceptibility is given by

χ⁡(ϵF)=−gv​gs3​π​e2​γ02​W|ϵF|.\chi(\epsilon_{F})=-\frac{g_{v}g_{s}}{3\pi}\,e^{2}\gamma_{0}^{2}\,\frac{W}{|\epsilon_{F}|}\,. (148)

In the clean limit the susceptibility is given by [254, 349, 213]:

χ⁡(ϵF)=−gv​gs6​π​e2​γ02​δ​(ϵF).\chi(\epsilon_{F})=-\frac{g_{v}g_{s}}{6\pi}\,e^{2}\gamma_{0}^{2}\,\delta(\epsilon_{F})\,. (149)

II.14 Spin orbit coupling

Spin-orbit coupling describes a process in which an electron changes simultaneously its spin and angular momentum or, in general, moves from one orbital wavefunction to another. The mixing of the spin and the orbital motion is a relativistic effect, which can be derived from Dirac’s model of the electron. It is large in heavy ions, where the average velocity of the electrons is higher. Carbon is a light atom, and the spin orbit interaction is expected to be weak.

The symmetries of the spin orbit interaction, however, allow the formation of a gap at the Dirac points in clean graphene. The spin orbit interaction leads to a spin dependent shift of the orbitals, which is of a different sign for the two sublattices, acting as an effective mass within each Dirac point [105, 192, 424]. The appearance of this gap leads to a non trivial spin Hall conductance, in similar way to other models which study the parity anomaly in relativistic field theory in (2+1) dimensions [162]. When the inversion symmetry of the honeycomb lattice is broken, either because the graphene layer is curved or because an external electric field is applied (Rashba interaction) additional terms, which modulate the nearest neighbor hopping, are induced [19]. The intrinsic and extrinsic spin orbit interactions can be written as [105, 192]:

ℋS​O;i​n​t\displaystyle{\cal H}_{SO;int}\!\! ≡\displaystyle\equiv Δs​o​∫d2​𝐫​Ψ^†​(𝐫)​s^z​σ^z​τ^z​Ψ^​(𝐫),\displaystyle\!\!\Delta_{so}\int d^{2}{\bf r}\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}({\bf r})\hat{s}_{z}\hat{\sigma}_{z}\hat{\tau}_{z}\hat{\Psi}({\bf r})\,,
ℋS​O;e​x​t\displaystyle{\cal H}_{SO;ext}\!\! ≡\displaystyle\equiv λR​∫d2​𝐫​Ψ^†​(𝐫)​(−s^x​σ^y+s^y​σ^x​τ^z)​Ψ^​(𝐫),\displaystyle\!\!\lambda_{R}\int\!\!d^{2}{\bf r}\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}({\bf r})(-\hat{s}_{x}\hat{\sigma}_{y}\!\!+\!\!\hat{s}_{y}\hat{\sigma}_{x}\hat{\tau}_{z})\hat{\Psi}({\bf r})\,, (150)

where σ^\hat{\sigma} and τ^\hat{\tau} are Pauli matrices which describe the sublattice and valley degrees of freedom, and s^\hat{s} are Pauli matrices acting on actual spin space. Δs​o\Delta_{so} is the spin-orbit coupling and λR\lambda_{R} is the Rashba coupling.

The magnitude of the spin orbit coupling in graphene can be inferred from the known spin orbit coupling in the carbon atom. This coupling allows for transitions between the pzp_{z} and pxp_{x} and pyp_{y} orbitals. An electric field induces also transitions between the pzp_{z} and ss orbitals. These intra-atomic processes mix the π\pi and σ\sigma bands in graphene. Using second order perturbation theory, one obtains a coupling between the low energy states in the π\pi band. Tight-binding [181, 439] and band structure calculations [265, 438] give estimates for the intrinsic and extrinsic spin-orbit interactions in the range 0.01−0.20.01-0.2 K, and hence much smaller than the other energy scales in the problem (kinetic, interaction, and disorder).

III Flexural phonons, elasticity, and crumpling

Graphite, in the Bernal stacking configuration, is a layered crystalline solid with 4 atoms per unit cell. Its basic structure is essentially a repetition of the bilayer structure discussed earlier. The coupling between the layers, as we discussed, is weak and, therefore, graphene has been always the starting point for the discussion of phonons in graphite [429]. Graphene has two atoms per unit cell and if we consider graphene as strictly 2D it should have 2 acoustic modes (with dispersion ωac​(k)∝k\omega_{{\rm ac}}(k)\propto k as k→0k\to 0) and 2 optical modes (with dispersion ωop​(k)∝constant\omega_{{\rm op}}(k)\propto{\rm constant}, as k→0k\to 0) solely due to the in-plane translation and stretching of the graphene lattice. Nevertheless, graphene exists in the 3D space and hence the atoms can oscillate out-of-plane leading to 2 out-of-plane phonons (one acoustic and another optical) called flexural modes. The acoustic flexural mode has dispersion ωflex​(k)∝k2\omega_{{\rm flex}}(k)\propto k^{2} as k→0k\to 0 which represents the translation of the whole graphene plane (essentially a one atom thick membrane) in the perpendicular direction (free particle motion). The optical flexural mode represents the out-of-phase out-of-plane oscillation of the neighboring atoms. In first approximation, if we neglect the coupling between graphene planes, graphite has essentially the same phonon modes, albeit they are degenerate. The coupling between planes has two main effects: (1) it lifts the degeneracy of the phonon modes, and (2) leads to a strong suppression of the energy of the flexural modes. Theoretically, flexural modes should become ordinary acoustic and optical modes in a fully covalent 3D solid, but in practice, the flexural modes survive due to the fact the planes are coupled by weak van der Waals-like forces. These modes have been measured experimentally in graphite [429]. Graphene can also be obtained as a suspended membrane, that is, without a substrate, being supported only by a scaffold or bridging micron-scale gaps [60, 261, 262]. Figure 24 shows a suspended graphene sheet and an atomic resolution image of its crystal lattice.

Because the flexural modes disperse like k2k^{2} they dominate the behavior of structural fluctuations in graphene at low energies (low temperatures) and long wavelengths. It is instructive to understand how these modes appear from the point of view of elasticity theory [276, 76]. Consider, for instance, a graphene sheet in 3D and let us parameterize the position of the sheet relative of a fixed coordinate frame in terms of the in-plane vector 𝐫{\bf r} and the height variable h⁡(𝐫)h({\bf r}) so that a position in the graphene is given by the vector 𝐑=(𝐫,h⁡(𝐫)){\bf R}=({\bf r},h({\bf r})). The unit vector normal to the surface is given by:

𝐍=𝐳−∇h1+(∇h)2,\displaystyle{\bf N}=\frac{{\bf z}-\nabla h}{\sqrt{1+(\nabla h)^{2}}}\,, (151)

where ∇=(∂x,∂y)\nabla=(\partial_{x},\partial_{y}) is the 2D gradient operator, and 𝐳{\bf z} is the unit vector in the third direction. In a flat graphene configuration all the normal vectors are aligned and therefore ∇⋅𝐍=0\nabla\cdot{\bf N}=0. Deviations from the flat configuration requires misalignment of the normal vectors and costs elastic energy. This elastic energy can be written as:

E0=κ2​∫d2​𝐫​(∇⋅𝐍)2≈κ2​∫d2​𝐫​(∇2h)2\displaystyle E_{0}=\frac{\kappa}{2}\int d^{2}{\bf r}\left(\nabla\cdot{\bf N}\right)^{2}\approx\frac{\kappa}{2}\int d^{2}{\bf r}\left(\nabla^{2}h\right)^{2} (152)

where κ\kappa is the bending stiffness of graphene, and the expression in terms of h⁡(𝐫)h({\bf r}) is valid for smooth distortions of the graphene sheet ((∇h)2≪1(\nabla h)^{2}\ll 1). The energy (152) is valid in the absence of a surface tension or a substrate which break the rotational and translational symmetry of the problem, respectively. In the presence of tension there is an energy cost for solid rotations of the graphene sheet (∇h≠0\nabla h\neq 0) and hence a new term has to be added to the elastic energy:

ET=γ2​∫d2​𝐫​(∇h)2,\displaystyle E_{{\rm T}}=\frac{\gamma}{2}\int d^{2}{\bf r}\left(\nabla h\right)^{2}\,, (153)

where γ\gamma is the interfacial stiffness. A substrate, described by a height variable s⁡(𝐫)s({\bf r}), pins the graphene sheet through van der Waals and other electrostatic potentials so that the graphene configuration tries to follow the substrate h⁡(𝐫)∼s⁡(𝐫)h({\bf r})\sim s({\bf r}). Deviations from this configuration cost extra elastic energy that can be approximated by a harmonic potential [398]:

ES=v2​∫d2​𝐫​(s⁡(𝐫)−h⁡(𝐫))2,\displaystyle E_{{\rm S}}=\frac{v}{2}\int d^{2}{\bf r}\left(s({\bf r})-h({\bf r})\right)^{2}\,, (154)

where vv characterizes the strength of the interaction potential between substrate and graphene.

Firstly, let us consider the free floating graphene problem (152) that we can rewrite in momentum space as:

E0=κ2​∑𝐤k4​h−𝐤​h𝐤.\displaystyle E_{0}=\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{{\bf k}}k^{4}h_{-{\bf k}}h_{{\bf k}}\,. (155)

We now canonically quantize the problem by introducing a momentum operator P𝐤P_{{\bf k}} that has the following commutator with h𝐤h_{{\bf k}}:

[h𝐤,P𝐤′]=i​δ𝐤,𝐤′,\displaystyle\left[h_{{\bf k}},P_{{\bf k^{\prime}}}\right]=i\delta_{{\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}}\,, (156)

and write the Hamiltonian as:

H=∑𝐤{P−𝐤​P𝐤2​σ+κ​k42​h−𝐤​h𝐤},\displaystyle H=\sum_{{\bf k}}\left\{\frac{P_{-{\bf k}}P_{{\bf k}}}{2\sigma}+\frac{\kappa k^{4}}{2}h_{-{\bf k}}h_{{\bf k}}\right\}\,, (157)

where σ\sigma is graphene’s 2D mass density. From the Heisenberg equations of motion for the operators it is trivial to find that h𝐤h_{{\bf k}} oscillates harmonically with a frequency given by:

ωflex​(𝐤)=(κσ)1/2​k2,\displaystyle\omega_{{\rm flex}}({\bf k})=\left(\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}\right)^{1/2}k^{2}\,, (158)

which is the long wavelength dispersion of the flexural modes. In the presence of tension it is easy to see that the dispersion is modified to:

ω⁡(𝐤)=k​κσ​k2+γσ,\displaystyle\omega({\bf k})=k\,\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}k^{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\sigma}}\,, (159)

indicating that the dispersion of the flexural modes becomes linear in kk, as k→0k\to 0, under tension. That is what happens in graphite where the interaction between layers breaks the rotational symmetry of the graphene layers.

Eq. (158) also allows us to relate the bending energy of graphene with the Young modulus, YY, of graphite. The fundamental resonance frequency of a macroscopic graphite sample of thickness tt is given by [60]:

ν⁡(𝐤)=(Yρ)1/2​t​k2,\displaystyle\nu({\bf k})=\left(\frac{Y}{\rho}\right)^{1/2}\,t\,k^{2}\,, (160)

where ρ=σ/t\rho=\sigma/t is the 3D mass density. Assuming that (160) works down to the single plane level, that is, when tt is the distance between planes, we find:

κ=Y​t3,\displaystyle\kappa=Yt^{3}\,, (161)

which provides a simple relationship between the bending stiffness and the Young modulus. Given that Y≈1012Y\approx 10^{12} N/m and t≈3.4t\approx 3.4 Å  we find, κ≈1\kappa\approx 1 eV. This result is in good agreement with ab initio calculations of the bending rigidity [228, 407] and experiments in graphene resonators [60].

The problem of structural order of a “free floating” graphene sheet can be fully understood from the existence of the flexural modes. Consider, for instance, the number of flexural modes per unit of area at a certain temperature TT:

Nph=∫d2​𝐤(2​π)2​n𝐤=12​π​∫0∞d​k​keβ​κ/σ​k2−1\displaystyle N_{{\rm ph}}=\int\frac{d^{2}{\bf k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}n_{{\bf k}}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}dk\frac{k}{e^{\beta\sqrt{\kappa/\sigma}k^{2}}-1} (162)

where n𝐤n_{{\bf k}} is the Bose-Einstein occupation number (β=1/(kB​T)\beta=1/(k_{B}T)). For T≠0T\neq 0 the above integral is logarithmically divergent in the infrared (k→0k\to 0) indicating a divergent number of phonons in the thermodynamic limit. For a system with finite size LL the smallest possible wave vector is of the order of kmin∼2​π/Lk_{{\rm min}}\sim 2\pi/L. Using kmink_{{\rm min}} as a lower cut-off in the integral (162) we find:

Nph=πLT2​ln⁡(11−e−L2T/L2),\displaystyle N_{{\rm ph}}=\frac{\pi}{L^{2}_{{\rm T}}}\ln\left(\frac{1}{1-e^{-L^{2}_{{\rm T}}/L^{2}}}\right)\,, (163)

where

LT=2​πkB​T​(κσ)1/4,\displaystyle L_{{\rm T}}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{k_{B}T}}\left(\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}\right)^{1/4}\,, (164)

is the thermal wavelength of the flexural modes. Notice that that when L≫LTL\gg L_{{\rm T}} the number of flexural phonons in (163) diverges logarithmically with the size of the system:

Nph≈2​πLT2​ln⁡(LLT),\displaystyle N_{{\rm ph}}\approx\frac{2\pi}{L^{2}_{{\rm T}}}\ln\left(\frac{L}{L_{{\rm T}}}\right)\,, (165)

indicating that the system cannot be structurally ordered at any finite temperature. This is nothing but the crumpling instability of soft membranes [276, 76]. For L≪LTL\ll L_{{\rm T}} one finds that NphN_{{\rm ph}} goes to zero exponentially with the size of the system indicating that systems with finite size can be flat at sufficiently low temperatures. Notice that for κ≈1\kappa\approx 1 eV, ρ≈2200\rho\approx 2200 kg/m3, t=3.4t=3.4 Å (σ≈7.5×10−7\sigma\approx 7.5\times 10^{-7} kg/m2), and T≈300T\approx 300 K, we find LT≈1L_{{\rm T}}\approx 1 Å  indicating that free floating graphene should always crumple at room temperature due to thermal fluctuations associated with flexural phonons. Nevertheless, the previous discussion only involves the harmonic (quadratic part) of the problem. Non-linear effects such as large bending deformations [313], the coupling between flexural and in-plane modes (or phonon-phonon interactions [52, 332]) and the presence of topological defects [277] can lead to strong renormalizations of the bending rigidity, driving the system toward a flat phase at low temperatures [76]. This situation has been confirmed in numerical simulations of free graphene sheets [116, 8].

The situation is rather different if the system is under tension or in the presence of a substrate or scaffold that can hold the graphene sheet. In fact, static rippling of graphene flakes suspended on scaffolds have been observed for single layer as well as bilayers [261, 262]. In this case the dispersion, in accordance with (159), is at least linear in kk, and the integral in (162) converges in the infrared (k→0k\to 0) indicating that the number of flexural phonons is finite and graphene does not crumple. We should notice that these thermal fluctuations are dynamic and hence average to zero over time, therefore, the graphene sheet is expected to be flat under these circumstances. Obviously, in the presence of a substrate or scaffold described by (154) static deformations of the graphene sheet are allowed. Also, hydrocarbon molecules that are often present on top of free hanging graphene membranes could quench flexural fluctuations making them static.

Finally, one should notice that in the presence of a metallic gate the electron-electron interactions lead to the coupling of the phonon modes to the electronic excitations in the gate. This coupling could be partially responsible to the damping of the phonon modes due to dissipative effects [363] as observed in graphene resonators [60].

IV Disorder in graphene

Graphene is a remarkable material from the electronic point of view. Because of the robustness and specificity of the sigma bonding, it is very hard for alien atoms to replace the carbon atoms in the honeycomb lattice. This is one of the reasons why the electron mean free path in graphene can be so long, reaching up to one micrometer in the existing samples. Nevertheless, graphene is not immune to disorder and its electronic properties are controlled by extrinsic as well as intrinsic effects that are unique to this system. Among the intrinsic sources of disorder we can highlight: surface ripples and topological defects. Extrinsic disorder can come about in many different forms: adatoms, vacancies, charges on top of graphene or in the substrate, and extended defects such as cracks and edges.

It is easy to see that from the point of view of single electron physics (that is, terms that can be added to (5)), there are two main terms that disorder couples to. The first one is a local change in the single site energy,

Hdd=∑iVi​(ai†​ai+bi†​bi),\displaystyle H_{{\rm dd}}=\sum_{i}V_{i}\left(a^{{\dagger}}_{i}a_{i}+b^{{\dagger}}_{i}b_{i}\right)\,, (166)

where ViV_{i} is the strength of the disorder potential on site 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i}, which is diagonal in the sublattice indices and hence, from the point of view of the Dirac Hamiltonian (28), can be written as:

Hdd=∫d2​r​∑a=1,2Va​(𝐫)​Ψ^a†​(𝐫)​Ψ^a​(𝐫),\displaystyle H_{{\rm dd}}=\int d^{2}r\sum_{a=1,2}V_{a}({\bf r})\hat{\Psi}^{{\dagger}}_{a}({\bf r})\hat{\Psi}_{a}({\bf r})\,, (167)

which acts as a chemical potential shift for the Dirac fermions, that is, shifts locally the Dirac point.

Because of the vanishing of the density of states in single layer graphene, and by consequence the lack of electrostatic screening, charge potentials may be rather important in determining the spectroscopic and transport properties [21, 288, 7]. Of particular importance is the Coulomb impurity problem where,

Va​(r)=e2ϵ0​1r,\displaystyle V_{a}(r)=\frac{e^{2}}{\epsilon_{0}}\frac{1}{r}\,, (168)

where ϵ0\epsilon_{0} is the dielectric constant of the medium. The solution of the Dirac equation for the Coulomb potential in 2D can be studied analytically [102, 373, 316, 48, 289]. Its solution has many of the features of the 3D relativistic hydrogen atom problem [38]. Just as in the case of the 3D problem the nature of the eigenfunctions depends strongly on graphene’s dimensionless coupling constant:

g=Z​e2ϵ0​vF.\displaystyle g=\frac{Ze^{2}}{\epsilon_{0}v_{F}}\,. (169)

Notice, therefore, that the coupling constant can be varied by either changing the charge of the impurity, ZZ, or modifying the dielectric environment and changing ϵ0\epsilon_{0}. For g<gc=1/2g<g_{c}=1/2 the solutions of this problem are given in terms of Coulomb wavefunctions with logarithmic phase shifts. The local density of states (LDOS) is affected close to the impurity due the electron-hole asymmetry generated by the Coulomb potential. The local charge density decays like 1/r31/r^{3} plus fast oscillations of the order of the lattice spacing (in the continuum limit this would give rise to a Dirac delta function for the density [208]). Just like in 3D QED, the 2D problem becomes unstable for g>gc=1/2g>g_{c}=1/2 leading to super-critical behavior and the so-called fall of electron to the center [219]. In this case the LDOS is strongly affected by the presence of the Coulomb impurity with the appearance of bound states outside the band and scattering resonances within the band [316] and the local electronic density decays monotonically like 1/r21/r^{2} at large distances.

It has been argued [358] that without high vacuum environment these Coulomb effects can be strongly suppressed by large effective dielectric constants due to the presence of a nanometer thin layer of absorbed water [346]. In fact, experiments in ultra-high vacuum conditions [85] display strong scattering features in the transport that can be associated to charge impurities. Screening effects that affect the strength and range of the Coulomb interaction, are rather non-trivial in graphene [369, 122] and, therefore, important for the interpretation of transport data [35, 286, 354, 229].

Another type of disorder is the one that changes the distance or angles between the pzp_{z} orbitals. In this case, the hopping energies between different sites are modified leading to a new term to the original Hamiltonian (5):

Hod\displaystyle H_{{\rm od}} =\displaystyle= ∑i,j{δti​j(a​b)(ai†bj+h.c.)\displaystyle\sum_{i,j}\left\{\delta t^{(ab)}_{ij}\left(a^{{\dagger}}_{i}b_{j}+{\rm h.c.}\right)\right. (170)
+\displaystyle+ δti​j(a​a)(ai†aj+bi†bj)},\displaystyle\left.\delta t^{(aa)}_{ij}\left(a^{{\dagger}}_{i}a_{j}+b^{{\dagger}}_{i}b_{j}\right)\right\}\,,

or in Fourier space:

Hod\displaystyle H_{{\rm od}} =\displaystyle= ∑𝐤,𝐤′a𝐤†​b𝐤′​∑i,δ→a​bδ​ti(a​b)​ei⁡(𝐤−𝐤′)⋅𝐑i−i​δ→a​a⋅𝐤′+h.c.\displaystyle\sum_{{\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}}a^{{\dagger}}_{{\bf k}}b_{{\bf k^{\prime}}}\sum_{i,\vec{\delta}_{ab}}\delta t^{(ab)}_{i}e^{i({\bf k}-{\bf k^{\prime}})\cdot{\bf R}_{i}-i\vec{\delta}_{aa}\cdot{\bf k^{\prime}}}+{\rm h.c.} (171)
+\displaystyle+ (a𝐤†​a𝐤′+b𝐤†​b𝐤′)​∑i,δ→a​aδ​ti(a​a)​ei⁡(𝐤−𝐤′)⋅𝐑i−i​δ→a​b⋅𝐤′,\displaystyle\!\!\!\left(\!a^{{\dagger}}_{{\bf k}}a_{{\bf k^{\prime}}}\!\!+\!\!b^{{\dagger}}_{{\bf k}}b_{{\bf k^{\prime}}}\!\right)\sum_{i,\vec{\delta}_{aa}}\delta t^{(aa)}_{i}e^{i({\bf k}-{\bf k^{\prime}})\cdot{\bf R}_{i}-i\vec{\delta}_{ab}\cdot{\bf k^{\prime}}},

where δ​ti​j(a​b)\delta t^{(ab)}_{ij} (δ​ti​j(a​a)\delta t^{(aa)}_{ij}) is the change of the hopping energy between orbitals on lattice sites 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i} and 𝐑j{\bf R}_{j} on the same (different) sublattices (we have written 𝐑j=𝐑i+δ→{\bf R}_{j}={\bf R}_{i}+\vec{\delta} where δ→a​b\vec{\delta}_{ab} is the nearest neighbor vector, and δ→a​a\vec{\delta}_{aa} is the next nearest neighbor vector). Following the procedure of Sec. II.2 we project out the Fourier components of the operators close to the K and K’ points of the BZ using (17). If we assume that δ​ti​j\delta t_{ij} is smooth over the lattice spacing scale, that is, it does not have an Fourier component with momentum 𝐊−𝐊′{\bf K}-{\bf K^{\prime}} (so the two Dirac cones are not coupled by disorder), we can rewrite (171) in real space as:

Hod\displaystyle H_{{\rm od}} =\displaystyle= ∫d2r[𝒜(𝐫)a1†(𝐫)b1(𝐫)+h.c.\displaystyle\int d^{2}r\left[{\cal A}({\bf r})a^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf r})b_{1}({\bf r})+{\rm h.c.}\right. (172)
+\displaystyle+ ϕ(𝐫)(a1†(𝐫)a1(𝐫)+b1†(𝐫)b1(𝐫))],\displaystyle\left.\phi({\bf r})\left(a^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf r})a_{1}({\bf r})+b^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf r})b_{1}({\bf r})\right)\right]\,,

with a similar expression for the cone 22 but with 𝒜{\cal A} replaced by 𝒜∗{\cal A}^{*}, where,

𝒜⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle{\cal A}({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= ∑δ→a​bδt(a​b)(𝐫)e−iδ→a​b⋅𝐊,\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{\delta}_{ab}}\delta t^{(ab)}({\bf r})e^{-i\vec{\delta}_{ab}\cdot{\bf K}}\,, (173)
ϕ⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle\phi({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= ∑δ→a​aδt(a​a)(𝐫)e−iδ→a​a⋅𝐊.\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{\delta}_{aa}}\delta t^{(aa)}({\bf r})e^{-i\vec{\delta}_{aa}\cdot{\bf K}}\,. (174)

Notice that whereas ϕ​(𝐫)=ϕ∗​(𝐫)\phi({\bf r})=\phi^{*}({\bf r}), because of the inversion symmetry of the two triangular sublattices that make up the honeycomb lattice, 𝒜{\cal A} is complex because of lack of inversion symmetry for nearest neighbor hopping. Hence,

𝒜⁡(𝐫)=𝒜x​(𝐫)+i​𝒜y​(𝐫).\displaystyle{\cal A}({\bf r})={\cal A}_{x}({\bf r})+i{\cal A}_{y}({\bf r})\,. (175)

In terms of the Dirac Hamiltonian (28) we can rewrite (172) as:

Hod\displaystyle H_{{\rm od}} =\displaystyle= ∫d2r[Ψ^1†(𝐫)𝝈⋅𝒜→(𝐫)Ψ^1(𝐫)\displaystyle\int d^{2}r\left[\hat{\Psi}^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf r})\bm{\sigma}\cdot\vec{{\cal A}}({\bf r})\hat{\Psi}_{1}({\bf r})\right. (176)
+\displaystyle+ ϕ(𝐫)Ψ^1†(𝐫)Ψ^1(𝐫)],\displaystyle\left.\phi({\bf r})\hat{\Psi}^{{\dagger}}_{1}({\bf r})\hat{\Psi}_{1}({\bf r})\right]\,,

where 𝒜→=(𝒜x,𝒜y)\vec{{\cal A}}=({\cal A}_{x},{\cal A}_{y}). This result shows that changes in the hopping amplitude lead to the appearance of vector, 𝒜→\vec{{\cal A}}, and scalar, Φ\Phi, potentials in the Dirac Hamiltonian. The presence of a vector potential in the problem indicates that an effective magnetic field B→=c/(evF)∇×𝒜→\vec{B}=c/(ev_{F})\nabla\times\vec{{\cal A}} should also be present, naively implying a broken time reversal symmetry, although the original problem was time reversal invariant. This broken time reversal symmetry is not real since (176) is the Hamiltonian around only one of the Dirac cones. The second Dirac cone is related to the first by time reversal symmetry indicating that the effective magnetic field is reversed in the second cone. Therefore, there is no global broken symmetry but a compensation between the two cones.

IV.1 Ripples

Graphene is a one atom thick system, the extreme case of a soft membrane. Hence, just like soft membranes, it is subject to distortions of its structure either due to thermal fluctuations (as we discussed in Sec. III) or interaction with a substrate, scaffold, and absorbands [398]. In the first case the fluctuations are time dependent (although with time scales much longer than the electronic ones), while in the second case the distortions act as quenched disorder. In both cases, the disorder comes about because of the modification of the distance and relative angle between the carbon atoms due to the bending of the graphene sheet. This type of off-diagonal disorder does not exist in ordinary 3D solids, or even in quasi-1D or quasi-2D systems, where atomic chains and atomic planes, respectively, are embedded in a 3D crystalline structure. In fact, graphene is also very different from other soft membranes because it is (semi) metallic, while previously studied membranes were insulators.

The problem of the bending of graphitic systems and its effect on the hybridization of the π\pi orbitals has been studied a great deal in the context of classical minimal surfaces [228] and applied to fullerenes and carbon nanotubes [400, 444, 432, 407, 190]. In order to understand the effect of bending on graphene, consider the situation shown in Fig.25. The bending of the graphene sheet has three main effects: the decrease of the distance between carbon atoms, a rotation of the pZp_{Z} orbitals (compression or dilation of the lattice are energetically costly due to the large spring constant of graphene ≈57\approx 57 eV/Å2 [432]), and a re-hybridization between π\pi and σ\sigma orbitals [115]. Bending by a radius RR decreases the distance between the orbitals from ℓ\ell to d=2​R​sin⁡[ℓ/(2​R)]≈ℓ−ℓ3/(24​R2)d=2R\sin[\ell/(2R)]\approx\ell-\ell^{3}/(24R^{2}) for R≫ℓR\gg\ell. The decrease in the distance between the orbitals increases the overlap between the two lobes of the pZp_{Z} orbital [165]: Vp​p​a≈Vp​p​a0​[1+ℓ2/(12​R2)]V_{ppa}\approx V_{ppa}^{0}[1+\ell^{2}/(12R^{2})], where a=π,σa=\pi,\sigma, and Vp​p​a0V_{ppa}^{0} is the overlap for a flat graphene sheet. The rotation of the pZp_{Z} orbitals can be understood within the Slater-Koster formalism, namely, the rotation can be decomposed into a pz−pzp_{z}-p_{z} (π\pi bond) plus a px−pxp_{x}-p_{x} (σ\sigma bond) hybridization with energies Vp​p​πV_{pp\pi} and Vp​p​σV_{pp\sigma}, respectively [165]: V⁡(θ)=Vp​p​π​cos2⁡(θ)−Vp​p​σ​sin2⁡(θ)≈Vp​p​π−(Vp​p​π+Vp​p​σ)​(ℓ/(2​R))2V(\theta)=V_{pp\pi}\cos^{2}(\theta)-V_{pp\sigma}\sin^{2}(\theta)\approx V_{pp\pi}-(V_{pp\pi}+V_{pp\sigma})(\ell/(2R))^{2}, leading to a decrease in the overlap. Furthermore, the rotation leads to re-hybridization between π\pi and σ\sigma orbitals leading to a further shift in energy of the order of [115]: δ​ϵπ≈(Vs​p​σ2+Vp​p​σ2)/(ϵπ−ϵa)\delta\epsilon_{\pi}\approx(V^{2}_{sp\sigma}+V^{2}_{pp\sigma})/(\epsilon_{\pi}-\epsilon_{a}).

In the presence of a substrate, as we discussed in Sec.III, elasticity theory predicts that graphene can be expected to follow the substrate in a smooth way. Indeed, by minimizing the elastic energy (152), (153), and (154) with respect to the height hh we get [398]:

κ​∇4h​(𝐫)−γ​∇2h​(𝐫)+v​h​(𝐫)=v​s​(𝐫),\displaystyle\kappa\nabla^{4}h({\bf r})-\gamma\nabla^{2}h({\bf r})+vh({\bf r})=vs({\bf r})\,, (177)

that can be solved by Fourier transform:

h⁡(𝐤)=s⁡(𝐤)1+(ℓt​k)2+(ℓc​k)4,\displaystyle h({\bf k})=\frac{s({\bf k})}{1+(\ell_{t}k)^{2}+(\ell_{c}k)^{4}}\,, (178)

where

ℓt\displaystyle\ell_{t} =\displaystyle= (γv)1/2,\displaystyle\left(\frac{\gamma}{v}\right)^{1/2}\,,
ℓc\displaystyle\ell_{c} =\displaystyle= (κv)1/4.\displaystyle\left(\frac{\kappa}{v}\right)^{1/4}\,. (179)

Eq. (178) gives the height configuration in terms of the substrate profile, and ℓt\ell_{t} and ℓc\ell_{c} provide the length scales for elastic distortion of graphene on a substrate. Hence, disorder in the substrate translates into disorder in the graphene sheet (albeit restricted by elastic constraints). This picture has been confirmed by STM measurements on graphene [391, 184] in which strong correlations were found between the roughness of the substrate and the graphene topography. Ab initio band structure calculations also give support to this scenario [99].

The connection between the ripples and the electronic problem comes from the relation between the height field h⁡(𝐫)h({\bf r}) and the local curvature of the graphene sheet, RR:

2R⁡(𝐫)≈∇2h​(𝐫),\displaystyle\frac{2}{R({\bf r})}\approx\nabla^{2}h({\bf r})\,, (180)

and, hence we see that due to bending the electrons are subject to a potential which depends on the structure of a graphene sheet [115]:

V⁡(𝐫)≈V0−α​(∇2h​(𝐫))2,\displaystyle V({\bf r})\approx V^{0}-\alpha\,(\nabla^{2}h({\bf r}))^{2}\,, (181)

where α\alpha (α≈10\alpha\approx 10 eV Å2) is the constant that depends on microscopic details. The conclusion from (181) is that the Dirac fermions are scattered by ripples of the graphene sheet through a potential which is proportional to the square of the local curvature. The coupling between geometry and electron propagation is unique to graphene, and results in additional scattering and resistivity due to ripples [198].

IV.2 Topological lattice defects

Structural defects of the honeycomb lattice like pentagons, heptagons and their combinations such as Stone-Wales defect (a combination of two pentagon-heptagon pairs) are also possible in graphene and can lead to scattering [90, 89]. These defects induce long range deformations, which modify the electron trajectories.

Let us consider first a disclination. This defect is equivalent to the deletion or inclusion of a wedge in the lattice. The simplest one in the honeycomb lattice is the absence of a 60∘60^{\circ} wedge. The resulting edges can be glued in such a way that all sites remain three-fold coordinated. The honeycomb lattice is recovered everywhere, except at the apex of the wedge, where a fivefold ring, a pentagon, is formed. One can imagine a situation where the nearest neighbor hoppings are unchanged. Nevertheless, the existence of a pentagon implies that the two sublattices of the honeycomb structure can no longer be defined. A trajectory around the pentagon after a closed circuit has to change the sublattice index.

The boundary conditions imposed at the edges of a disclination are sketched in Fig. 26, showing the identification of sites from different sublattices. In addition, the wavefunctions at the KK and K′K^{\prime} points are exchanged when moving around the pentagon.

Far away from the defect, a slow rotation of the components of the spinorial wavefunction can be described by a gauge field which acts on the valley and sublattice indices [142, 144]. This gauge field is technically non-abelian, although a transformation can be defined which makes the resulting Dirac equation equivalent to one with an effective abelian gauge field [144]. The final continuum equation gives a reasonable description of the electronic spectrum of fullerenes of different sizes [142, 144], and other structures which contain pentagons [222, 305, 206, 217, 207]. It is easy to see that an heptagon leads to the opposite effective field.

An in-plane dislocation, that is, the inclusion of a semi-infinite row of sites, can be considered as induced by a pentagon and a heptagon together. The non-abelian field described above is canceled away from the core. A closed path implies a shift by one (or more) lattice spacings. The wavefunctions at the KK and K′K^{\prime} points acquire phases, e±2πi/3e^{\pm 2\pi i/3}, under a translation by one lattice unit. Hence, the description of a dislocation in the continuum limit requires an (abelian) vortex of charge ±2π/3\pm 2\pi/3 at its core. Dislocations separated over distances of the order of dd lead to an effective flux through an area of perimeter ll of the order of [269]:

Φ∼dkF​l2\Phi\sim\frac{d}{k_{\rm F}l^{2}} (182)

where kFk_{\rm F} is the Fermi vector of the electrons.

In general, a local rotation of the axes of the honeycomb lattice induces changes in the hopping which lead to mixing of the KK and K′K^{\prime} wavefunctions, leading to a gauge field like the one induced by a pentagon [148]. Graphene samples with disclinations and dislocations are feasible in particular substrates [91], and gauge fields related to the local curvature are then expected to play a crucial role in such structures. The resulting electronic structure can be analyzed using the theory of quantum mechanics in curved space [47, 90, 89, 189].

IV.3 Impurity states

Point defects, similar to impurities and vacancies, can nucleate electronic states in their vicinity. Hence, a concentration of nin_{i} impurities per carbon atom leads to a change in the electronic density of the order of nin_{i}. The corresponding shift in the Fermi energy is ϵF≃vF​ni\epsilon_{\rm F}\simeq v_{\rm F}\sqrt{n_{i}}. In addition, impurities lead to a finite elastic mean free path, lelas≃ani−1/2l_{\rm elas}\simeq an_{i}^{-1/2}, and to an elastic scattering time τelas≃(vF​ni)−1\tau_{\rm elas}\simeq(v_{\rm F}n_{i})^{-1}. Hence, the regions with few impurities can be considered low-density metals in the dirty limit, as τelas−1≃ϵF\tau_{\rm elas}^{-1}\simeq\epsilon_{\rm F}.

The Dirac equation allows for localized solutions that satisfy many possible boundary conditions. It is known that small circular defects result in localized and semi-localized states [103], that is, states whose wavefunction decays as 1/r1/r as a function of the distance from the center of the defect. A discrete version of these states can be realized in a nearest neighbor tight-binding model with unitary scatterers such as vacancies [314]. In the continuum, the Dirac equation (29) for the wavefunction, ψ⁡(𝐫)=(ϕ1​(𝐫),ϕ2​(𝐫))\psi({\bf r})=(\phi_{1}({\bf r}),\phi_{2}({\bf r})), can be written as:

∂wϕ1​(w,w∗)\displaystyle\partial_{w}\phi_{1}(w,w^{*}) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0\,,
∂w∗ϕ2​(w,w∗)\displaystyle\partial_{w^{*}}\phi_{2}(w,w^{*}) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0\,, (183)

where w=x+i​yw=x+iy is a complex number. These equations indicate that at zero energy the components of the wavefunction can only be either holomorphic or anti-holomorphic with respect to the variable ww (that is, ϕ1​(w,w∗)=ϕ1​(w∗)\phi_{1}(w,w^{*})=\phi_{1}(w^{*}) and ϕ2​(w,w∗)=ϕ2​(w)\phi_{2}(w,w^{*})=\phi_{2}(w)). Since the boundary conditions require that the wavefunction vanishes at infinity the only possible solutions have the form: ΨK​(𝐫→)∝(1/(x+i​y)n,0)\Psi_{K}({\bf\vec{r}})\propto(1/(x+iy)^{n},0) or ΨK′​(𝐫→)∝(0,1/(x−i​y)n)\Psi_{K^{\prime}}({\bf\vec{r}})\propto(0,1/(x-iy)^{n}). The wavefunctions in the discrete lattice must be real, and at large distances the actual solution found near a vacancy tends to a superposition of two solutions formed from wavefunctions from the two valleys with equal weight, in a way similar to the mixing at armchair edges [58].

The construction of the semi-localized state around a vacancy in the honeycomb lattice can be extended to other discrete models which leads to the Dirac equation in the continuum limit. A particular case is the nearest neighbor square lattice with half flux per plaquette, or the nearest neighbor square lattice with two flavors per site. The latter has been extensively studied in relation to the effects of impurities on the electronic structure of d-wave superconductors [33], and numerical results are in agreement with the existence of this solution. As the state is localized on one sublattice only, the solution can be generalized for the case of two vacancies.

IV.4 Localized states near edges, cracks, and voids

Localized states can be defined at edges where the number of atoms in the two sublattices is not compensated. The number of them depend on details of the edge. The graphene edges can be strongly deformed, due to the bonding of other atoms to carbon atoms at the edges. These atoms should not induce states in the graphene π\pi band. In general, a boundary inside the graphene material will exist, as sketched in Fig. 27, beyond which the s​p2sp^{2} hybridization is well defined. If this is the case, the number of mid-gap states near the edge is roughly proportional to the difference in sites between the two sublattices near this boundary.

Along a zigzag edge there is one localized state per three lattice units. This implies that a precursor structure for localized states at the Dirac energy can be found in ribbons or constrictions of small lengths [271], which modifies the electronic structure and transport properties.

Localized solutions can also be found near other defects that contain broken bonds or vacancies. These states do not allow an analytical solution, although, as discussed above, the continuum Dirac equation is compatible with many boundary conditions, and it should describe well localized states that vary slowly over distances comparable to the lattice spacing. The existence of these states can be investigated by analyzing the scaling of the spectrum near a defect as a function of the size of the system, LL [419]. A number of small voids and elongated cracks show states whose energy scales as L−2L^{-2}, while the energy of extended states scales as L−1L^{-1}. A state with energy scaling L−2L^{-2} is compatible with continuum states for which the modulus of the wavefunction decays as r−2r^{-2} as a function of the distance from the defect.

IV.5 Self-doping

The band structure calculations discussed in previous sections show that the electronic structure of a single graphene plane is not strictly symmetrical in energy [335]. The absence of electron-hole symmetry shifts the energy of the states localized near impurities above or below the Fermi level, leading to a transfer of charge from/to the clean regions. Hence, the combination of localized defects and the lack of perfect electron-hole symmetry around the Dirac points leads to the possibility of self-doping, in addition to the usual scattering processes.

Extended lattice defects, like edges, grain boundaries, or micro-cracks, are likely to induce a number of electronic states proportional to their length, L/aL/a, where aa is of the order of the lattice constant. Hence, a distribution of extended defects of length LL at a distance equal to LL itself gives rise to a concentration of L/aL/a carriers per carbon in regions of size of the order of (L/a)2(L/a)^{2}. The resulting system can be considered a metal with a low density of carriers, ncarrier∝a/Ln_{\rm carrier}\propto a/L per unit cell, and an elastic mean free path lelas≃Ll_{\rm elas}\simeq L. Then, we obtain:

ϵF\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm F} ≃\displaystyle\simeq vFa​L\displaystyle\frac{v_{\rm F}}{\sqrt{aL}}
1τelas\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{{\rm elas}}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq vFL\displaystyle\frac{v_{\rm F}}{L} (184)

and, therefore, (τelas)−1≪ϵF(\tau_{{\rm elas}})^{-1}\ll\epsilon_{\rm F} when a/L≪1a/L\ll 1. Hence, the existence of extended defects leads to the possibility of self-doping but maintaining most of the sample in the clean limit. In this regime, coherent oscillations of transport properties are expected, although the observed electronic properties may correspond to a shifted Fermi energy with respect to the nominally neutral defect–free system.

One can describe the effects that break electron-hole symmetry near the Dirac points in terms of a finite next-nearest neighbor hopping between π\pi orbitals, t′t^{\prime}, in (174). Consider, for instance, electronic structure of a ribbon of width LL terminated by zigzag edges, which, as discussed, lead to surface states for t′=0t^{\prime}=0. The translational symmetry along the axis of the ribbon allows us to define bands in terms of a wavevector parallel to this axis. On the other hand, the localized surface bands, extending from k∥=(2​π)/3k_{\parallel}=(2\pi)/3 to k∥=−(2π)/3k_{\parallel}=-(2\pi)/3 acquire a dispersion of order t′t^{\prime}. Hence, if the Fermi energy remains unchanged at the position of the Dirac points (ϵDirac=−3​t′\epsilon_{\rm Dirac}=-3t^{\prime}), this band will be filled, and the ribbon will no longer be charge neutral. In order to restore charge neutrality, the Fermi level needs to be shifted by an amount of the order of t′t^{\prime}. As a consequence, some of the extended states near the Dirac points are filled, leading to the phenomenon of self-doping. The local charge is a function of distance to the edges, setting the Fermi energy so that the ribbon is globally neutral. Note that the charge transferred to the surface states is mostly localized near the edges of the system.

The charge transfer is suppressed by electrostatic effects, as large deviations from charge neutrality have an associated energy cost [322]. In order to study these charging effects we add to the free-electron Hamiltonian (5) the Coulomb energy of interaction between electrons:

HI=∑i,jUi,j​ni​nj,\displaystyle H_{I}=\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}n_{i}n_{j}\,, (185)

where ni=∑σ(ai,σ†​ai,σ+bi,σ†​bi,σ)n_{i}=\sum_{\sigma}(a^{{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma}a_{i,\sigma}+b^{{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma}b_{i,\sigma}) is the number operator at site 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i}, and

Ui,j=e2ϵ0​|𝐑i−𝐑j|,\displaystyle U_{i,j}=\frac{e^{2}}{\epsilon_{0}|{\bf R}_{i}-{\bf R}_{j}|}\,, (186)

is the Coulomb interaction between electrons. We expect, on physics grounds, that an electrostatic potential builds up at the edges, shifting the position of the surface states, and reducing the charge transferred to/from them. The potential at the edge induced by a constant doping δ\delta per carbon atom is roughly, ∼(δ​e2/a)​(W/a)\sim(\delta e^{2}/a)(W/a) (δ​e2/a\delta e^{2}/a is the Coulomb energy per carbon), and WW the width of the ribbon (W/aW/a is the number of atoms involved). The charge transfer is stopped when the potential shifts the localized states to the Fermi energy, that is, when t′≈(e2/a)​(W/a)​δt^{\prime}\approx(e^{2}/a)(W/a)\delta. The resulting self-doping is therefore

δ∼t′​a2e2​W,\displaystyle\delta\sim\frac{t^{\prime}a^{2}}{e^{2}W}\,, (187)

that vanishes when W→∞W\to\infty.

We treat Hamiltonian (185) within the Hartree approximation (that is, we replace HIH_{I} by HM.F.=∑iVi​niH_{{\rm M.F.}}=\sum_{i}V_{i}n_{i} where Vi=∑jUi,j​⟨nj⟩V_{i}=\sum_{j}U_{i,j}\langle n_{j}\rangle, and solve the problem self-consistently for ⟨ni⟩\langle n_{i}\rangle). Numerical results for graphene ribbons of length L=80​3​aL=80\sqrt{3}a and different widths are shown in Fig. 28 (t′/t=0.2t^{\prime}/t=0.2 and e2/a=0.5​te^{2}/a=0.5t). The largest width studied is ∼0.1​μ\sim 0.1\mum, and the total number of carbon atoms in the ribbon is ≈105\approx 10^{5}. Notice that as WW increases, the self-doping decreases indicating that, for a perfect graphene plane (W→∞W\rightarrow\infty), the self-doping effect disappears. For realistic parameters, we find that the amount of self-doping is 10−4−10−510^{-4}-10^{-5} electrons per unit cell for sizes 0.1−1​μ0.1-1\mum.

IV.6 Vector potential and gauge field disorder

As discussed in Sec. IV, lattice distortions modify the Dirac equation that describes the low energy band structure of graphene. We consider here deformations that change slowly on the lattice scale, so that they do not mix the two inequivalent valleys. As shown earlier, perturbations that hybridize the two sublattices lead to terms that change the Dirac Hamiltonian from vF​𝝈⋅𝐤v_{F}\bm{\sigma}\cdot{\bf k} into vF​𝝈⋅𝐤+𝝈⋅𝐀v_{\rm F}\bm{\sigma}\cdot{\bf k}+\bm{\sigma}\cdot{\bf A}. Hence, the vector 𝐀{\bf A} can be thought of as if induced by an effective gauge field, 𝐀{\bf A}. In order to preserve time reversal symmetry, this gauge field must have opposite signs at the two Dirac cones, 𝐀K=−𝐀K′{\bf A}_{K}=-{\bf A}_{K^{\prime}}.

A simple example is a distortion that changes the hopping between all bonds along a given axis of the lattice. Let us assume that the sites at the ends of those bonds define the unit cell, as sketched in Fig. 29. If the distortion is constant, its only effect is to displace the Dirac points away from the BZ corners. The two inequivalent points are displaced in opposite directions. This uniform distortion is the equivalent of a constant gauge field, which does not change the electronic spectrum. The situation changes if one considers a boundary that separates two domains where the magnitude of the distortion is different. The shift of the Dirac points leads to a deflection of the electronic trajectories that cross the boundary, as also sketched in Fig. 29. The modulation of the gauge field leads to an effective magnetic field, which is of opposite sign for the two valleys.

We have shown in Section IV.2 how topological lattice defects, such as disclinations and dislocations, can be described by an effective gauge field. Those defects can only exist in graphene sheets that are intrinsically curved, and the gauge field only depends on topology of the lattice. Changes in the nearest neighbor hopping also lead to effective gauge fields. We consider next two physical processes that induce effective gauge fields: (i) changes in the hopping induced by hybridization between π\pi and σ\sigma bands, which arise in curved sheets, and (ii) changes in the hopping due to modulation in the bond length, which is associated with elastic strain. The strength of these fields depends on parameters that describe the value of the π\pi-σ\sigma hybridization, and the dependence of hopping on the bond length.

A comparison of the relative strengths of the gauge fields induced by intrinsic curvature, π−σ\pi-\sigma hybridization (extrinsic curvature), and elastic strains, arising from a ripple of typical height and size is given in Table 2.

IV.6.1 Gauge field induced by curvature

As we discussed in Sec. IV.1, when the π\pi orbitals are not parallel, the hybridization between them depends on their relative orientation. The angle θi\theta_{i} determines the relative orientation of neighboring orbitals at some position 𝐫i{\bf r}_{i} in the graphene sheet. The value of θi\theta_{i} depends on the local curvature of the layer. The relative angle of rotation of two pzp_{z} orbitals at position 𝐫i{\bf r}_{i} and 𝐫j{\bf r}_{j} can be written as: cos⁡(θi−θj)=𝐍i⋅𝐍j\cos(\theta_{i}-\theta_{j})={\bf N}_{i}\cdot{\bf N}_{j}, where 𝐍i{\bf N}_{i} is the unit vector perpendicular to the surface, defined in (151). If 𝐫j=𝐫i+𝐮i​j{\bf r}_{j}={\bf r}_{i}+{\bf u}_{ij} we can write:

𝐍i⋅𝐍j≈+𝐍i⋅[(𝐮i​j⋅∇)𝐍i]+12𝐍i⋅[(𝐮i​j⋅∇)2𝐍i],\displaystyle{\bf N}_{i}\!\cdot\!{\bf N}_{j}\!\approx\!1\!+\!{\bf N}_{i}\!\cdot\![({\bf u}_{ij}\!\cdot\!\nabla){\bf N}_{i}]\!+\!\frac{1}{2}{\bf N}_{i}\!\cdot\![({\bf u}_{ij}\!\cdot\!\nabla)^{2}{\bf N}_{i}]\,, (188)

where we assume smoothly varying 𝐍⁡(𝐫){\bf N}({\bf r}). We use (151) in terms of the height field h⁡(𝐫)h({\bf r}) (𝐍⁡(𝐫)≈𝐳−∇h​(𝐫)−(∇h)2​𝐳/2{\bf N}({\bf r})\approx{\bf z}-\nabla h({\bf r})-(\nabla h)^{2}{\bf z}/2) to rewrite (188) as:

𝐍i⋅𝐍j≈1−12[(𝐮i​j⋅∇)∇h(𝐫i)]2.\displaystyle{\bf N}_{i}\cdot{\bf N}_{j}\approx 1-\frac{1}{2}[({\bf u}_{ij}\cdot\nabla)\nabla h({\bf r}_{i})]^{2}\,. (189)

Hence, bending of the graphene sheet leads to a modification of the hopping amplitude between different sites in the form:

δti​j≈−ti​j02[(𝐮i​j⋅∇)∇h(𝐫i)]2,\displaystyle\delta t_{ij}\approx-\frac{t_{ij}^{0}}{2}[({\bf u}_{ij}\cdot\nabla)\nabla h({\bf r}_{i})]^{2}\,, (190)

where ti​j0t_{ij}^{0} is the bare hopping energy. A similar effect leads to changes the electronic states in a carbon nanotubes [190]. Using the results of Sec. IV, namely (173), we can now see that a vector potential is generated for nearest neighbor hopping (𝐮=δ→a​b{\bf u}=\vec{\delta}_{ab}) [115]:

𝒜x(h)\displaystyle{\cal A}^{(h)}_{x} =\displaystyle= −3​Ea​b​a28​[(∂x2h)2−(∂y2h)2]\displaystyle-\frac{3E_{ab}a^{2}}{8}\left[(\partial_{x}^{2}h)^{2}-(\partial_{y}^{2}h)^{2}\right]
𝒜y(h)\displaystyle{\cal A}^{(h)}_{y} =\displaystyle= 3​Ea​b​a24​(∂x2h+∂y2h)​∂xh​∂yh\displaystyle\frac{3E_{ab}a^{2}}{4}\left(\partial_{x}^{2}h+\partial_{y}^{2}h\right)\partial_{x}h\partial_{y}h (191)

where the coupling constant Ea​bE_{ab} depends on microscopic details [115]. The flux of effective magnetic field through a ripple of lateral dimension ll and height hh is given approximately by:

Φ≈Ea​b​a2​h2vF​l3\Phi\approx\frac{E_{ab}a^{2}h^{2}}{v_{\rm F}l^{3}} (192)

where the radius of curvature is R−1≈h​l−2R^{-1}\approx hl^{-2}. For a ripple with l≈20l\approx 20nm, h≈1h\approx 1nm, taking Ea​b/vF≈10E_{ab}/v_{\rm F}\approx 10 Å-1 , we find Φ≈10−3​Φ0\Phi\approx 10^{-3}\Phi_{0}.

IV.6.2 Elastic strain

The elastic free energy for graphene can be written in terms of the in-plane displacement 𝐮⁡(𝐫)=(ux,uy){\bf u}({\bf r})=(u_{x},u_{y}) as:

F⁡[𝐮]=12​∫d2​r​[(ℬ−𝒢)​(∑i=1,2ui​i)2+2​𝒢​∑i,j=1,2ui​j2],\displaystyle F[{\bf u}]\!=\!\frac{1}{2}\!\int\!d^{2}r\left[({\cal B}-{\cal G})(\sum_{i=1,2}u_{ii})^{2}+2{\cal G}\sum_{i,j=1,2}u^{2}_{ij}\right]\,, (193)

where ℬ{\cal B} is the bulk modulus, 𝒢{\cal G} is the shear modulus, and

ui​j=12​(∂ui∂xj+∂uj∂xj),\displaystyle u_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}+\frac{\partial u_{j}}{\partial x_{j}}\right)\,, (194)

is the strain tensor (x1=xx_{1}=x and x2=yx_{2}=y).

There are many types of static deformation of the honeycomb lattice which can affect the propagation of Dirac fermions. The simplest one is due to changes in the area of the unit cell either due to dilation or contraction. Changes in the unit cell area lead to local changes in the density of electrons and, therefore, local changes in the chemical potential in the system. In this case, their effect is similar to the one found in (174), and we must have:

ϕdp​(𝐫)=g⁡(ux​x+uy​y),\displaystyle\phi_{{\rm dp}}({\bf r})=g(u_{xx}+u_{yy})\,, (195)

and their effect is diagonal in the sublattice index.

The nearest neighbor hopping depends on the length of the carbon bond. Hence, elastic strains that modify the relative orientation of the atoms also lead to an effective gauge field, which acts on each KK point separately, as first discussed in relation to carbon nanotubes [397, 237]. Consider two carbon atoms located in two different sublattices in the same unit cell at 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i}. The change in the local bond length can be written as:

δ​ui=δ→a​ba⋅[𝐮A​(𝐑i)−𝐮B​(𝐑i+δ→a​b)].\displaystyle\delta u_{i}=\frac{\vec{\delta}_{ab}}{a}\cdot[{\bf u}_{{\rm A}}({\bf R}_{i})-{\bf u}_{{\rm B}}({\bf R}_{i}+\vec{\delta}_{ab})]\,. (196)

The local displacements of the atoms in the unit cell can be related to 𝐮⁡(𝐫){\bf u}({\bf r}) by [20]:

(δ→a​b⋅∇)𝐮=κ−1(𝐮A−𝐮B),\displaystyle(\vec{\delta}_{ab}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}=\kappa^{-1}({\bf u}_{{\rm A}}-{\bf u}_{{\rm B}})\,, (197)

where κ\kappa is a dimensionless quantity that depends on microscopic details. Changes in the bond length lead to changes in the hopping amplitude:

ti​j≈ti​j0+∂ti​j∂a​δ​ui,\displaystyle t_{ij}\approx t_{ij}^{0}+\frac{\partial t_{ij}}{\partial a}\delta u_{i}\,, (198)

and we can write:

δ​t(a​b)​(𝐫)≈β​δ​u​(𝐫)a,\displaystyle\delta t^{(ab)}({\bf r})\approx\beta\frac{\delta u({\bf r})}{a}\,, (199)

where

β=∂t(a​b)∂ln⁡(a).\displaystyle\beta=\frac{\partial t^{(ab)}}{\partial\ln(a)}\,. (200)

Substituting (196) into (199) and the final result into (173), one finds [20]:

𝒜x(s)\displaystyle{\cal A}^{(s)}_{x} =\displaystyle= 34​β​κ​(ux​x−uy​y),\displaystyle\frac{3}{4}\beta\,\kappa\,(u_{xx}-u_{yy})\,,
𝒜y(s)\displaystyle{\cal A}^{(s)}_{y} =\displaystyle= 32​β​κ​ux​y.\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}\beta\,\kappa\,u_{xy}\,. (201)

We assume that the strains induced by a ripple of dimension ll and height hh scale as ui​j∼(h/l)2u_{ij}\sim(h/l)^{2}. Then, using β/vF≈a−1∼1\beta/v_{\rm F}\approx a^{-1}\sim 1Å-1, we find that the total flux through a ripple is:

Φ≈h2a​l.\Phi\approx\frac{h^{2}}{al}\,. (202)

For ripples such that h∼1h\sim 1nm and l∼20l\sim 20nm, this estimate gives Φ∼10−1​Φ0\Phi\sim 10^{-1}\Phi_{0} in reasonable agreement with the estimates in ref. [267].

The strain tensor must satisfy some additional constraints, as it is derived from a displacement vector field. These constraints are called Saint Venant compatibility conditions [218]:

Wi​j​k​l=∂ui​j∂xk​∂xl+∂uk​l∂xi​∂xj−∂ui​l∂xj​∂xk−∂uj​k∂xi​∂xl=0.W_{ijkl}=\frac{\partial u_{ij}}{\partial x_{k}\partial x_{l}}+\frac{\partial u_{kl}}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}-\frac{\partial u_{il}}{\partial x_{j}\partial x_{k}}-\frac{\partial u_{jk}}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{l}}=0\,. (203)

An elastic deformation changes the distances in the crystal lattice and can be considered as a change in the metric:

gi​j=δi​j+ui​jg_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+u_{ij} (204)

The compatibility equations (203) are equivalent to the condition that the curvature tensor derived from (204) is zero. Hence, a purely elastic deformation cannot induce intrinsic curvature in the sheet, which only arises from topological defects. The effective fields associated with elastic strains can be large [267], leading to significant changes in the electronic wavefunctions. An analysis of the resulting state, and the possible instabilities that may occur can be found in [155].

IV.6.3 Random gauge fields

The preceding discussion suggests that the effective fields associated with lattice defects can modify significantly the electronic properties. This is the case when the fields do not change appreciably on scales comparable to the (effective) magnetic length. The general problem of random gauge fields for Dirac fermions has been extensively analyzed before the current interest in graphene, as the topic is also relevant for the IQHE [234] and d-wave superconductivity [278]. The one electron nature of this two dimensional problem makes it possible, at the Dirac energy, to map it onto models of interacting electrons in one dimension, where many exact results can be obtained [69]. The low energy density of states, ρ⁡(ω)\rho(\omega), acquires an anomalous exponent, ρ⁡(ω)∝|ω|1−Δ\rho(\omega)\propto|\omega|^{1-\Delta}, where Δ>0\Delta>0. The density of states is enhanced near the Dirac energy, reflecting the tendency of disorder to close gaps. For sufficiently large values of the random gauge field, a phase transition is also possible [78, 178].

Perturbation theory shows that random gauge fields are a marginal perturbation at the Dirac point, leading to logarithmic divergences. These divergences tend to have the opposite sign with respect to those induced by the Coulomb interaction (see Sec. V.2). As a result, a renormalization group (RG) analysis of interacting electrons in a random gauge field suggests the possibility of non-trivial phases [124, 125, 286, 388, 203, 14, 11, 98], where interactions and disorder cancel each other.

IV.7 Coupling to magnetic impurities

Magnetic impurities in graphene can be introduced chemically by deposition and intercalation [411, 61], or self-generated by the introduction of defects [214, 215]. The energy dependence of the density of states in graphene leads to changes in the formation of a Kondo resonance between a magnetic impurity and the graphene electrons. The vanishing of the density of states at the Dirac energy implies that a Kondo singlet in the ground state is not formed unless the exchange coupling exceeds a critical value, of the order of the electron bandwidth, a problem already studied in connection with magnetic impurities in d-wave superconductors [67, 68, 330, 331, 128]. For weak exchange couplings, the magnetic impurity remains unscreened. An external gate changes the chemical potential, allowing for a tuning of the Kondo resonance [362]. The situation changes significantly if the scalar potential induced by the magnetic impurity is taken into account. This potential that can be comparable to the bandwidth allows the formation of mid-gap states and changes the phase-shift associated to spin scattering [170]. These phase-shifts have a weak logarithmic dependence on the chemical potential, and a Kondo resonance can exist, even close to the Dirac energy.

The RKKY interaction between magnetic impurities is also modified in graphene. At finite fillings, the absence of intra-valley backscattering leads to a reduction of the Friedel oscillations, which decay as sin⁡(2​kF​r)/|r|3\sin(2k_{\rm F}r)/|r|^{3} [82, 431, 21]. This effect leads to an RKKY interaction, at finite fillings, which oscillate and decay as |r|−3|r|^{-3}. When intervalley scattering is included, the interaction reverts to the usual dependence on distance in two dimensions, |r|−2|r|^{-2} [82]. At half-filling extended defects lead to an RKKY interaction with an |r|−3|r|^{-3} dependence [419, 109]. This behavior is changed when the impurity potential is localized on atomic scales [355, 59], or for highly symmetrical couplings [355].

IV.8 Weak and strong localization

In sufficiently clean systems, where the Fermi wavelength is much shorter than the mean free path, kF​l≫1k_{\rm F}l\gg 1, electronic transport can be described in classical terms, assuming that electrons follow well defined trajectories. At low temperatures, when electrons remain coherent over long distances, quantum effects lead to interference corrections to the classical expressions for the conductivity, the weak localization correction [43, 77]. These corrections are usually due to the positive interference between two paths along closed loops, traversed in opposite directions. As a result, the probability that the electron goes back to the origin is enhanced, so that quantum corrections decrease the conductivity. These interferences are suppressed for paths longer than the dephasing length, lϕl_{\phi}, determined by interactions between the electron and environment. Interference effects can also be suppressed by magnetic fields that break down time reversal symmetry and adds a random relative phase to the process discussed above. Hence, in most metals, the conductivity increases when a small magnetic field is applied (negative magnetoresistance).

Graphene is special in this respect, due to the chirality of its electrons. The motion along a closed path induces a change in the relative weight of the two components of the wavefunction, leading to a new phase, which contributes to the interference processes. If the electron traverses a path without being scattered from one valley to the other, this (Berry) phase changes the sign of the amplitude of one path with respect to the time-reversed path. As a consequence, the two paths interfere destructively, leading to a suppression of backscattering [396]. Similar processes take place in materials with strong spin orbit coupling, as the spin direction changes along the path of the electron [43, 77]. Hence, if scattering between valleys in graphene can be neglected, one expects a positive magnetoresistance, i. e., weak anti-localization. In general, intra- and intervalley elastic scattering can be described in terms of two different scattering times, τi​n​t​r​a\tau_{intra} and τi​n​t​e​r\tau_{inter}, so that if τi​n​t​r​a≪τi​n​t​e​r\tau_{intra}\ll\tau_{inter} one expects weak anti-localization processes, while if τi​n​t​e​r≪τi​n​t​r​a\tau_{inter}\ll\tau_{intra} ordinary weak localization will take place. Experimentally, localization effects are always strongly suppressed close to the Dirac point but can be partially or, in rare cases, completely recovered at high carrier concentrations, depending on a particular single-layer sample [267, 401]. Multilayer samples exhibit an additional positive magnetoresistance in higher magnetic fields, which can be attribued to classical changes in the current distribution due to a vertical gradient of concentration [267] and anti-localization effects [430].

The propagation of an electron in the absence of intervalley scattering can be affected by the effective gauge fields induced by lattice defects and curvature. These fields can suppress the interference corrections to the conductivity [267, 269]. In addition, the description in terms of free Dirac electrons is only valid near the neutrality point. The Fermi energy acquires a trigonal distortion away from the Dirac point, and backward scattering within each valley is no longer completely suppressed [253], leading to a further suppression of anti-localization effects at high dopings. Finally, the gradient of external potentials induce a small asymmetry between the two sublattices [269]. This effect will also contribute to reduce anti-localization, without giving rise to localization effects.

The above analysis has to be modified for a graphene bilayer. Although the description of the electronic states requires a two component spinor, the total phase around a closed loop is 2​π2\pi, and backscattering is not suppressed [201]. This result is consistent with experimental observations, which show the existence of weak localization effects in a bilayer [149].

When the Fermi energy is at the Dirac point, a replica analysis shows that the conductivity approaches a universal value of the order of e2/he^{2}/h [126, 127]. This result is valid when intervalley scattering is neglected [307, 308, 345]. Localization is induced when these terms are included [14, 11], as also confirmed by numerical calculations [233]. Interaction effects tend to suppress the effects of disorder. The same result, namely a conductance of the order of e2/he^{2}/h, is obtained for disordered graphene bilayers where a self-consistent calculation leads to universal conductivity at the neutrality point [281, 282, 197]. In a biased graphene bilayer, the presence of impurities leads to the appearance of impurity tails in the density of states due to the creation of mid-gap states which are sensitive to the applied electric field that opens the gap between the conduction and valence bands [280].

One should point out that most of the calculations of transport properties assume self-averaging, that is, that one can exchange a problem with lack of translational invariance by an effective medium system with damping. Obviously this procedure only works when the disorder is weak and the system is in the metallic phase. Close to the localized phase this procedure breaks down, the system divides itself into regions of different chemical potential and one has to think about transport in real space, usually described in terms of percolation [83, 369]. Single electron transistor (SET) measurements of graphene show that this seems to be the situation in graphene at half-filling [247].

Finally, we should point out that graphene stacks suffer from another source of disorder, namely, c-axis disorder that is either due to impurities between layers or rotation of graphene planes relative to each other. In either case the in-plane and out-of-plane transport is directly affected. This kind of disorder has been observed experimentally by different techniques [167, 34]. In the case of the bilayer, the rotation of planes changes substantially the spectrum restoring the Dirac fermion description [232]. The transport properties in the out of plane direction are determined by the interlayer current operator, 𝐣^n,n+1=i​t​∑(cA,n,s†​cA,n+1,s−cA,n+1,s†​cA,n,s)\hat{\bf j}_{n,n+1}=it\sum(c_{A,n,s}^{\dagger}c_{A,n+1,s}-c_{A,n+1,s}^{\dagger}c_{A,n,s}), where nn is a layer index, and AA is a generic index that defines the sites coupled by the interlayer hopping tt. If we only consider hopping between nearest neighbor sites in consecutive layers, these sites belong to one of the two sublattices in each layer.

In a multilayer with Bernal stacking, these connected sites are the ones where the density of states vanishes at zero energy, as discussed above. Hence, even in a clean system, the number of conducting channels in the direction perpendicular to the layers vanishes at zero energy [281, 282]. This situation is reminiscent of the in plane transport properties of a single layer graphene. Similar to the latter case, a self-consistent Born approximation for a small concentration of impurities leads to a finite conductivity, which becomes independent of the number of impurities.

IV.9 Transport near the Dirac point

In clean graphene, the number of channels available for electron transport decreases as the chemical potential approaches the Dirac energy. As a result, the conductance through a clean graphene ribbon is, at most, 4​e2/h4e^{2}/h, where the factor of 4 stands for the spin and valley degeneracy. In addition, only one out of every three possible clean graphene ribbons have a conduction channel at the Dirac energy. The other two thirds are semiconducting, with a gap of the order of vF/Wv_{\rm F}/W, where WW is the width. This result is a consequence of the additional periodicity introduced by the wavefunctions at the KK and K′K^{\prime} points of the Brillouin Zone, irrespective of the boundary conditions.

A wide graphene ribbon allows for many channels, which can be approximately classified by the momentum perpendicular to the axis of the ribbon, kyk_{y}. At the Dirac energy, transport through these channels is inhibited by the existence of a gap, Δky=vF​ky\Delta_{k_{y}}=v_{\rm F}k_{y}. Transport through these channels is suppressed by a factor of the order of e−ky​Le^{-k_{y}L}, where LL is the length of the ribbon. The number of transverse channels increases as W/aW/a, where WW is the width of the ribbon and aa is a length of the order of the lattice spacing. The allowed values of kyk_{y} are ∝ny/W\propto n_{y}/W, where nyn_{y} is an integer. Hence, for a ribbon such that W≫LW\gg L, there are many channels which satisfy ky​L≪1k_{y}L\ll 1. Transport through these channels is not strongly inhibited, and their contribution dominates when the Fermi energy lies near the Dirac point. The conductance arising from these channels is given approximately by [194, 409]:

G∼e2h​W2​π​∫d​ky​e−ky​L∼e2h​WL.G\sim\frac{e^{2}}{h}\frac{W}{2\pi}\int dk_{y}e^{-k_{y}L}\sim\frac{e^{2}}{h}\frac{W}{L}\,. (205)

The transmission at normal incidence, ky=0k_{y}=0, is one, in agreement with the absence of backscattering in graphene, for any barrier that does not induce intervalley scattering [200]. The transmission of a given channel scales as T⁡(ky)=1/cosh2⁡(ky​L/2)T(k_{y})=1/\cosh^{2}(k_{y}L/2).

Eq.(205) shows that the contribution from all transverse channels lead to a conductance which scales, similar to a function of the length and width of the system, as the conductivity of a diffusive metal. Moreover, the value of the effective conductivity is of the order of e2/he^{2}/h. It can also be shown that the shot noise depends on current in the same way as in a diffusive metal. A detailed analysis of possible boundary conditions at the contacts and their influence on evanescent waves can be found in [359, 336]. The calculations leading to eq.(205) can be extended to a graphene bilayer. The conductance is, again, a summation of terms arising from evanescent waves between the two contacts, and it has the dependence on sample dimensions of a 2D conductivity of the order of e2/he^{2}/h [379], although there is a prefactor twice bigger than the one in single layer graphene.
